provenancePages.text: 1 MEMORANDUM Department of Health and Human Services Public Health Service Food and Drug Administration Center for Drug Evaluation and Research ______________________________________________________________________ Date: August 19, 2020 From: Lois M. Freed, Ph.D. Supervisory Pharmacologist, Division of Neurology 2 Acting Director, Division of Pharmacology/Toxicology-Neuroscience Office of Neuroscience Subject: BLA 125326 (ofatumumab) ______________________________________________________________________ Ofatumumab (Arzerra), a fully human type 1 IgG1κ monoclonal antibody targeting CD20+ B cells, was originally approved on October 26, 2009, for the treatment of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL). The sponsor (Novartis Pharmaceuticals Corporation) submitted a Prior Approval Supplement to BLA 125326 on December 20, 2019, proposing a new indication for ofatumumab, relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis (RMS). Clinical development of ofatumumab for the treatment of RMS was conducted under IND 111116. For the new indication, the sponsor conducted pharmacology (proof-of-concept) and reproductive and developmental toxicology (male and female fertility and enhanced pre- and postnatal development [ePPND]) studies to support clinical development and marketing authorization. The Division agreed with the sponsor that a standard assessment of carcinogenic risk was not required because ofatumumab is not pharmacologically active in rodent species. The nonclinical studies submitted to support the new indication were reviewed by Dr. Melissa Banks-Muckenfuss (Pharmacology/Toxicology BLA Review and Evaluation, BLA 125326, Supplement 70, July 9, 2020). Dr. Banks-Muckenfuss also references previous reviews of the nonclinical data submitted to support approval of ofatumumab for CLL. The proposed mechanism by which ofatumumab exerts therapeutic effects in patients with RMS is through binding to CD20+ B cells (EC50 of 287 ng/mL) resulting in B-cell lysis, possibly through antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) and complement-dependent cytotoxicity (CDC). ADCC and CDC were demonstrated in in vitro assays with ofatumumab. In vivo studies demonstrated depletion of CD20+ B-cell populations in blood and lymphoid tissues following subcutaneous (SC) or intravenous (IV) administration of ofatumumab to cynomolgus monkeys. Reference ID: 4658998

provenancePages.text: 5 2 INTRODUCTION 2.1 Overview Buprenorphine is a partial opioid agonist and was first approved in 1981. Buprenorphine was first approved for the treatment of opioid dependence in 2002 under the trade names Subutex® and Suboxone®. CAM2038 consists of two different formulations of buprenorphine that are intended for use as a subcutaneous depot injection that were developed for the treatment of moderate to severe opioid use disorder, which is described in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5). The two formulations are designed to have different treatment intervals, with one formulation intended for weekly injection, and one for monthly injection. Each formulation was developed in four different doses with which the applicant intends to cover the entire range of doses commonly used for sublingual treatment. The applicant conducted a single clinical efficacy study which is summarized in Table 1. See Section 3.2 for a thorough discussion of this study. Table 1: List of all studies included in analysis Phase and Design Treatment Period Follow-up Period # of Patients per Arm Study Population HS-11-421 NCT# 02651584 Phase 3, Double-blind, double- dummy, active control 24 Weeks 1 month CAM2038: 213 SL BPN/NX: 215 New Entrants to treatment with Moderate to Severe Opioid Use Disorder The development program was conducted under Investigation New Drug (IND) application number 114,082 which was originally submitted by Braeburn on April 20, 2015. This was preceded by a Pre-IND that was submitted on December 5, 2001 by Camurus. I will now summarize any interactions between the applicant and the Agency where the design and analysis of the clinical efficacy study was discussed. The first interaction between the Agency and the applicant was a Pre-IND meeting that was held on March 13, 2012. At this meeting the design of the development program was discussed. This included discussion of the intended patient population for the study, the requirement for blinding of the study, the length of the study, and the intended endpoint for the study. The next meeting was the End of Phase 2 meeting which was held on February 24, 2015. During this meeting the applicant provided more details on their intended efficacy study. There was further discussion on the design and how the applicant expects CAM2038 to be utilized clinically. The proposed endpoint for the study was the proportion of negative urine opioid tests at month 3 and month 6. This was later modified to be an analysis of the proportion of responders in the study. On June 11, 2015, the development program was placed on clinical hold due to safety concerns including the sufficiency of the support for the proposed dose and duration of the clinical Reference ID: 4199935

6 efficacy study. On July 9, 2015, further comments were provided to the applicant regarding the design of the clinical efficacy study, including discussion on the selection of the clinical endpoint and the justification for the non-inferiority margin. The clinical hold was lifted on October 2, 2015. On October 22, 2015, the Agency provided further feedback on the design of the clinical efficacy study. Issues discussed included the applicant’s proposal for the responder definition and the non-inferiority margin. Now a responder was defined as a patient who had no evidence of illicit opioid use in at least 50% of the urines collected in the study after an initial grace period. The Agency stated that the applicant must provide a justification for this endpoint, or propose an alternative endpoint. The study was initiated on December 29, 2015. The applicant provided an amended version of the protocol in February 2016. The applicant further modified the responder definition to be as follows: No opioids detected in at least 33% of the twelve urine toxicology results in the first twelve weeks of the study and at least 67% of urine toxicology results collected during the final twelve weeks. The applicant also narrowed the non-inferiority margin from % to %. Further feedback was provided by the Agency on September 1, 2016. The Agency stated that there was insufficient historical evidence for the % non-inferiority margin and a more conservative approach with a 5% non-inferiority margin was proposed. On October 14, 2016, the applicant requested clarification on the selection of the non-inferiority margin prior to planned database lock on November 4th. As previously discussed, the agency had proposed a non-inferiority margin of 5% compared to the applicant’s previously proposed % margin. On November 4, 2016, the Agency provided a response to the applicant that a 10% margin would be acceptable. The Pre-NDA meeting for this application was held on March 16, 2017. 2.2 Data Sources The data was provided electronically by the Applicant as SAS transport files in the CDISC and ADaM data format. provenancePages.text: NDA/BLA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation NDA 213586 Uzedy (risperidone extended release injection) 25 Version date: July 7, 2019 3 Regulatory Background U.S. Regulatory Actions and Marketing History TV-46000 (risperidone extended-release injectable suspension for sc use) has not been approved or marketed in the United States. Risperdal (risperidone), the LD, was first approved in 1993 as tablets for oral administration for the treatment of schizophrenia in adults (NDA 20272). Currently, there are multiple additional dosage forms available for risperidone including: an injectable suspension for intramuscular use (NDA 21346; Risperdal Consta), oral solution (NDA Risperdal), an orally disintegrating tablet (NDA 021444; Risperdal M- Tab), and an injectable suspension for subcutaneous use (NDA 210655; Perseris). Summary of Presubmission/Submission Regulatory Activity On October 15, 2015, the Division met with the Sponsor for a pre-IND meeting. At that time, the Sponsor proposed to conduct a pharmacokinetic (PK) study to provide a scientific bridge to the proposed listed drug, Risperdal tablets (NDA 20272) and a phase 3 placebo-controlled efficacy study in patients with schizophrenia with a plan to submit a 505(b)(2) application. The Division agreed with the overall development plan, but stated that the proposed primary efficacy endpoint was not acceptable for the phase 3 efficacy study and the Sponsor agreed to use an endpoint of time to impending relapse. The Division met with the Sponsor in May 2017 for a Type C meeting to discuss changes to the phase 3 development plan and a plan to change the product presentation from a vial to a prefilled syringe (PFS). The Division agreed with the plan for a phase 3 efficacy study and open- label extension safety study and provided advice on conducting a comprehensive use-related risk analysis to inform the need for human factors studies. At an end-of-phase 1 meeting in December 2017, the Sponsor informed the Division that, based on the results of study TV-46000-SAD-10055, they planned to use a once monthly (q1m) regimen and change the planned once every three months (q3m) regimen to a once every two months (q2m) regimen in the planned efficacy study TV-46000-CNS-30072. The Division noted that, scientifically, matching peak and trough concentrations for a long-acting injection to those from an oral formulation to determine product dosing may not be a good strategy because it could result in trough levels lasting a few days or weeks that could confer a different risk of relapse. The Sponsor indicated their plan to continue the phase 3 study with the selected dosing regimens and committed to documenting and analyzing the timing of adverse events and relapse within the dosing interval. provenancePages.text: NDA # 213931 Elizabeth Hausner 6 IND120566 (DCN) hyperphosphatemia in patients with end stage renal disease NDA 211801(DG) IBSRELA® (tenapanor, 50 mg tablet) approved September 12, 2019 for treatment of irritable bowel syndrome with constipation (IBS-C) 2.7 Regulatory Background Tenapanor has also been known as RDX5791, AZ13667691, and AZD1722. The major metabolite (M1) is AZ13792925, representing >10% of the total tenapanor-related drug exposure in humans based on AUC. During the clinical development with tenapanor for IBS, the observation was made that tenapanor decreased urine phosphorous excretion and increased stool phosphorous excretion. The sponsor decided to explore the therapeutic potential of this effect. 3 Studies Not Reviewed The majority of nonclinical studies were reviewed during the IND stage. An inventory of the studies provided and reviewed are attached to this review as an appendix. Only those studies pertaining to the pharmacology for the present indication have been reviewed. The reader is referred to the Unireview available in DARRTS for NDA 211801 for a detailed evaluation of the nonclinical studies. 4 Pharmacology 4.1 Primary Pharmacology Tenapanor is proposed as an inhibitor of the sodium/hydrogen exchanger isoform 3(NHE3). By inhibiting NHE3 on the apical surface of enterocytes, tenapanor reduces the uptake of sodium from the lumen of the gastrointestinal tract, resulting in increased luminal fluid. Tenapanor has also been demonstrated to decrease urinary phosphorous excretion while increasing fecal phosphate excretion. Recently provided mechanistic studies (review entered into DARRTS February 2, 2020 for IND120566) suggest that passive paracellular absorption is reduced and that there is a modulation to the intercellular tight junctions manifested experimentally as increased transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER),thereby reducing paracellular phosphate Permeability. There have been species differences in tolerability of tenapanor, mainly due to susceptibility to intestinal fluid retention and diarrhea, which the sponsor summarized as follows: • Rat NOAEL <30 mg/kg/day in a 28-day repeat doses study Reference ID: 4709537 (b) (4) (b) (4)

provenancePages.text: NDA #214927 Kenrick M. Semple, Ph.D., DABT 3 1 Background 1.1 Regulatory History The Applicant, Zevra, Denmark AS is developing Arimoclomol citrate (Miplyffa) for Niemann-Pick Type C (NPC) Disease, a rare neurodegenerative disease, which is an inborn error of lipid metabolism that results from pathogenic mutations in the NPC1 or NPC2 genes. IND 124547 was submitted on May 9, 2016, by Orphazyme A/S (Orphazyme). Orphazyme received Orphan Drug designation for arimoclomol for treatment of NPC on January 13, 2015, Fast Track designation on June 24, 2016, and Breakthrough Therapy designation on November 18, 2019. Orphazyme submitted NDA 214927 for arimoclomol in three components for rolling review on May 28, 2020, June 30, 2020, and July 17, 2020. On June 17, 2021, the Division issued a Complete Response Letter (CRL). The Division listed the deficiencies in the CRL as the validity and reliability of the 5-Domain Niemann- Pick Type C (NPC) Disease Clinical Severity Scale (5DNPCCSS) and weak and contradictory confirmatory evidence of effectiveness. Nonclinical deficiencies included questionable clinical relevance of the in-vitro data, and lack of reproducible results in the submitted pharmacology studies (see FDA AC Briefing Document). On October 13, 2021, a Type A meeting was held with the Applicant as they sought guidance and concurrence with their plan to address the CRL deficiencies. The Division asked the Applicant to provide any additional nonclinical data that may be able to support efficacy. See nonclinical review (Dr. Miyun Tsai-Turton, November 4, 2021). On June 10, 2022, the sponsorship of IND 124547 and ownership of NDA 214927 was transferred from Orphazyme to KemPharm Denmark A/S (Kempharm). On April 13, 2023, the Applicant’s corporate name was changed to Zevra Denmark A/S (Zevra). On April 28, 2023, Zevra submitted a meeting request to discuss their additional nonclinical evidence, particularly non-clinical study reports and revised primary analysis plan to support a potential NDA resubmission. On May 1, 2023, the Division granted a virtual meeting scheduled for August 10, 2023. The meeting briefing package was received on July 11, 2023. The Division provided preliminary comments on August 8, 2023 and meeting minutes were issued on August 24, 2023. On December 21, 2023, the Applicant resubmitted the NDA (SDN 51) to address the deficiencies in the CRL. The NDA resubmission includes eight (8) new in vitro studies, three (3) new in vivo studies, and three (3) amended in vivo studies. These studies are reviewed herein. Reference ID: 5447492

Summary of Regulatory History On October 20, 2014, Orphazyme A/S (Orphazyme) submitted a pre-IND meeting request to the Division of Gastroenterology and Inborn Errors Products to discuss the development program for arimoclomol for the treatment of NPC. The meeting took place on December 17, 2014. The FDA provided feedback on the overall development program, including study design, nonclinical, clinical pharmacology, and product quality strategy. The meeting minutes were issued on December 19, 2014. On January 13, 2015, Orphazyme received orphan drug designation for arimoclomol for the treatment of NPC. Orphazyme returned for a pre-IND type C meeting on January 12, 2016, to discuss their proposed pivotal Phase 2/3 trial. The discussion focused on the proposed primary endpoint, NPCCSS. The FDA raised concerns about the challenges of interpreting a composite scoring of 17 domains in the NPCCSS and on the instrument’s reliability and validity. The FDA also commented on the proposed study duration, dosing, and concomitant use of miglustat, statistical methods, carcinogenicity study, and Chemistry, Manufacturing, and Controls (CMC) plan. The meeting minutes were issued on February 16, 2016. IND 124547 was received along with a Fast Track designation request on May 9, 2016. The IND contained a natural history protocol, Study CT-ORZY-NPC-001 titled “A Prospective Non- Therapeutic Study in Patients Diagnosed With Niemann-Pick Disease Type C in Order to Characterize the Individual Patient Disease Profile and Historic Signo-Symptomatology Progression Pattern” and a phase 2/3 protocol for Study CT-ORZY-NPC-002 (henceforth referred to as Study NPC-002) titled “Arimoclomol Prospective Double-Blind, Randomized, Placebo-Controlled Study in Patients Diagnosed With Niemann-Pick Disease Type C.” The studies were determined to be safe to proceed although the FDA continued to have concerns with the clinical development plan. Comments were provided in the ‘Study May Proceed’ letter issued on June 2, 2016. Fast Track designation was granted on June 24, 2016. The FDA had multiple follow-up interactions with the applicant to discuss its concerns on the proposed use of a total score from the NPCCSS measurement instrument as the primary endpoint in Study NPC-002. In order to generate interpretable data to support efficacy, the FDA suggested that the Applicant focus on the domains that capture the core symptoms/signs of NPC where a meaningful change of improvement can be demonstrated. Communications provided included an emailed Information Request dated September 2, 2016, and an advice letter dated January 19, 2017. During a follow-up type B guidance meeting on July 20, 2017, Orphazyme proposed a revised primary endpoint of the five-domain Niemann-Pick disease type C Clinical Severity Scale (5DNPCCSS), including ambulation, swallow, fine motor skills, cognition, and speech. The FDA expressed that the proposed change is reasonable although the issues identified in the previous interactions, such as establishing the instrument’s validity and scoring standardization, had not been addressed. Meeting minutes were issued on August 7, 2017. On January 18, 2018, Orphazyme received a Rare Pediatric disease designation for arimoclomol. Reference ID: 4813446

NDA 214927 arimoclomol 124 Integrated Review Template, version 2.0 (04/23/2020) In an advice letter issued on January 7, 2020, the FDA confirmed that additional nonclinical studies are not needed to assess the abuse potential of arimoclomol. The FDA suggested that Orphazyme continue to monitor for abuse-related adverse events throughout the clinical development program. Due to an FDA reorganization in early 2020, IND 124547 transitioned from the Division of Gastroenterology and Inborn Errors Products to the Division of Rare Diseases and Medical Genetics (DRDMG). Orphazyme met with DRDMG in an initial comprehensive multidisciplinary breakthrough guidance meeting on March 10, 2020. The Division denied Orphazyme’s request to defer the thorough QT (TQT) study until after NDA approval because nonclinical and clinical data suggested a possible QT safety signal. The Division did accept that the TQT final study report could be provided as a late submission, along with previously agreed to late submissions for renal and hepatic impairment studies. Concerns regarding the potential impurity control were also discussed. Additional feedback on the proposed data package for a biowaiver request were provided. The meeting minutes were issued on March 18, 2020. On April 22, 2020, Orphazyme submitted a response to address the FDA’s concern on the proposed level in the drug product. Based on the additional information provided, the FDA concluded that the proposed acceptable intake of in the drug substance arimoclomol ( ng/day) is acceptable. The Applicant was notified of this agreement via email on May 21, 2020. A rolling review designation for Orphazyme’s intended 505(b)(1) NDA submission was requested on March 24, 2020, and granted on March 25, 2020. The pre-NDA meeting took place on April 16, 2020, wherein Orphazyme informed that the TQT study was at risk for delay due to the COVID-19 pandemic. The Division denied Orphazyme’s request to further delay the TQT study report submission. In addition, the proposed primary estimand for Study NPC-002 was not agreed upon due to concerns that it relied upon statistical methods for handling hypothetical data. Meeting minutes were issued on April 17, 2020. On October 14, 2020, the final protocol for Study NPC-002 (version 10.0) and Investigator’s Brochure v4.0 were submitted. In this amendment, Orphazyme indicated that the CYP2D6 inhibition is not clinically relevant. NDA 214927 for arimoclomol was submitted in three components: CMC modules received May 28, 2020, nonclinical modules received June 30, 2020, and clinical modules received July 17, 2020. The Division determined that the NDA would receive a priority review because arimoclomol is intended to treat a serious disease with no approved therapy. Orphazyme submitted the final TQT study report late in the review cycle on December 22, 2020. The Division determined this submission to be a major amendment to the application and, on December 23, 2020, informed Orphazyme that it was extending the user fee goal date by three months from March 17, 2021, to June 17, 2021. Adequacy of Carcinogenicity Study The Division considers the transgenic mouse study an adequate assessment of carcinogenic potential because the high dose of arimoclomol was based on an MTD. The Division asked the Applicant to provide any additional nonclinical data that may be able to support efficacy. See nonclinical review (Dr. Miyun Tsai-Turton, November 4, 2021). On June 10, 2022, the sponsorship of IND 124547 and ownership of NDA 214927 was transferred from Orphazyme to KemPharm Denmark A/S (Kempharm). On April 13, 2023, the Applicant’s corporate name was changed to Zevra Denmark A/S (Zevra). On April 28, 2023, Zevra submitted a meeting request to discuss their additional nonclinical evidence, particularly non-clinical study reports and revised primary analysis plan to support a potential NDA resubmission. On May 1, 2023, the Division granted a virtual meeting scheduled for August 10, 2023. The meeting briefing package was received on July 11, 2023. The Division provided preliminary comments on August 8, 2023 and meeting minutes were issued on August 24, 2023. On December 21, 2023, the Applicant resubmitted the NDA (SDN 51) to address the deficiencies in the CRL. The NDA resubmission includes eight (8) new in vitro studies, three (3) new in vivo studies, and three (3) amended in vivo studies. These studies are reviewed herein. Reference ID: 5447492

provenancePages.text: NDA 214927 arimoclomol 124 Integrated Review Template, version 2.0 (04/23/2020) In an advice letter issued on January 7, 2020, the FDA confirmed that additional nonclinical studies are not needed to assess the abuse potential of arimoclomol. The FDA suggested that Orphazyme continue to monitor for abuse-related adverse events throughout the clinical development program. Due to an FDA reorganization in early 2020, IND 124547 transitioned from the Division of Gastroenterology and Inborn Errors Products to the Division of Rare Diseases and Medical Genetics (DRDMG). Orphazyme met with DRDMG in an initial comprehensive multidisciplinary breakthrough guidance meeting on March 10, 2020. The Division denied Orphazyme’s request to defer the thorough QT (TQT) study until after NDA approval because nonclinical and clinical data suggested a possible QT safety signal. The Division did accept that the TQT final study report could be provided as a late submission, along with previously agreed to late submissions for renal and hepatic impairment studies. Concerns regarding the potential impurity control were also discussed. Additional feedback on the proposed data package for a biowaiver request were provided. The meeting minutes were issued on March 18, 2020. On April 22, 2020, Orphazyme submitted a response to address the FDA’s concern on the proposed level in the drug product. Based on the additional information provided, the FDA concluded that the proposed acceptable intake of in the drug substance arimoclomol ( ng/day) is acceptable. The Applicant was notified of this agreement via email on May 21, 2020. A rolling review designation for Orphazyme’s intended 505(b)(1) NDA submission was requested on March 24, 2020, and granted on March 25, 2020. The pre-NDA meeting took place on April 16, 2020, wherein Orphazyme informed that the TQT study was at risk for delay due to the COVID-19 pandemic. The Division denied Orphazyme’s request to further delay the TQT study report submission. In addition, the proposed primary estimand for Study NPC-002 was not agreed upon due to concerns that it relied upon statistical methods for handling hypothetical data. Meeting minutes were issued on April 17, 2020. On October 14, 2020, the final protocol for Study NPC-002 (version 10.0) and Investigator’s Brochure v4.0 were submitted. In this amendment, Orphazyme indicated that the CYP2D6 inhibition is not clinically relevant. NDA 214927 for arimoclomol was submitted in three components: CMC modules received May 28, 2020, nonclinical modules received June 30, 2020, and clinical modules received July 17, 2020. The Division determined that the NDA would receive a priority review because arimoclomol is intended to treat a serious disease with no approved therapy. Orphazyme submitted the final TQT study report late in the review cycle on December 22, 2020. The Division determined this submission to be a major amendment to the application and, on December 23, 2020, informed Orphazyme that it was extending the user fee goal date by three months from March 17, 2021, to June 17, 2021. provenancePages.text: NDA 214927 arimoclomol 15 Integrated Review Template, version 2.0 (04/23/2020) diagnosed with mild or moderate Gaucher disease (GD) when enzyme replacement therapy is not a therapeutic option (FDA 2020b). Outside of the United States, miglustat has been approved for the treatment of the progressive neurologic manifestations of NPC disease in pediatric and adult patients (EMC 2020). Miglustat is often prescribed “off-label” for patients in the United States, as evidenced by the large number of patients (approximately 80%) enrolled in the arimoclomol development program, who were receiving miglustat at baseline. Given the rarity of NPC disease, there is limited availability of patients to enroll in randomized trials. Trial participation is also compounded by an emerging preference for enrollment in open- label or expanded access studies, which are study designs that can introduce significant concerns for bias that limits the interpretation of results (Hastings et al. 2019). NDA 021348 (miglustat) Actelion Clinical Research, Inc. (NDA 021348) propose NPC disease as a new labeling indication for miglustat. At the time of the sNDA submission, miglustat product labeling contained a ‘Warnings and Precautions’ section that described peripheral neuropathy, tremor (30% of patients), and osmotic diarrhea and weight loss (85% and 65% of patients, respectively) for patients with type 1 GD. The primary endpoint of the prospective study in NDA 021348 was defined as the change from baseline to month 12 in horizontal saccadic eye movement velocity (HSEM-α). The application was discussed at an Advisory Committee Meeting on January 12, 2010. Ultimately, the application received a Complete Response on March 8, 2010. Because of the high rate of off-label use of miglustat in the NPC patient population, subgroup analyses for miglustat in both the efficacy and safety data were requested by the division in this NDA submission. Regulatory History The development program of arimoclomol for the treatment of NPC was conducted under IND 124547. During the pre-IND meeting on January 12, 2016, discussion focused on the Agency’s concern that the initial proposal to conduct a single, open-label phase 2/3 study with an external control would not be adequate or well-controlled, and would not address the Agency’s concerns regarding dose selection. Completion of juvenile animal toxicology studies were also needed to support trial duration. The division requested an assessment for abuse potential of arimoclomol based upon concern that nonclinical studies noted evidence of neurotoxicity (tremor and convulsions). Exploratory biomarker data, such as Lyso-SM-509, would also be important to obtain during such a trial. The data by Solomon et al. suggest a minimum of three to four years disease progression prior to the appearance of consistent changes in the ability of swallow. In a new, placebo controlled study using arimoclomol, the comparison of functional testing could be used as supportive data if a strong correlation was identified between the PAS and ASHA-NOMS swallow scale, as similarly demonstrated by Solomon et al. In summary, the statistical analyses of study NPC-002 result in a small difference in the 5DNPCCSS score between the treatment and placebo arms, though additional nonclinical, mechanistic, biomarker and natural history data submitted to the NDA do not provide a clear understanding of the clinical relevance of this result. It is the opinion of this medical officer that this NDA should receive a complete response because the data to support the use of arimoclomol in patients diagnosed with NPC are not robust and, ultimately, do not meet the Agency’s usual evidentiary standards for effectiveness. The use of regulatory flexibility for this rare, progressive, neurodegenerative disorder can certainly be considered by other members of the review team. Body weight gain in the group receiving 1350 mg/kg/day was lower (-56-64%) than the controls during days 1-8. The ECAC concurred with the Sponsor’s proposed high dose of 750 mg/kg BID, which demonstrated saturation of exposure at 6 weeks, and was also considered to be the MTD based on mortality observed at 2000 mg/kg/day (QD) in the 2-week toxicity study (Study Report No. GB07MB). The Committee recommended 250 mg/kg and 100 mg/kg BID as the mid- and low dose, respectively, to allow for adequate spacing of the AUC between doses. Prior FDA ExecCAC Dose Concurrence? Yes, under IND 124547, with ECAC SPA Agreement dated October 22, 2019. The study was conducted at the agreed upon doses. Mouse Carcinogenicity Conclusion: Negative Mouse Tumor Findings (details): The tumor data were analyzed by the FDA statistical reviewer, Feng Zhou, for dose response relationships across the vehicle control group, and low, mid, and high dose groups, and pairwise comparisons of each of the three treated groups against the vehicle control group for both male and female mice. Excluding the positive control group, the tumor data analysis showed a positive dose response for the rare tumor, hemangioma, and the combination of hemangioma with hemangiosarcoma in the spleen and whole body in female mice when compared with the vehicle control group (P<0.05). By pairwise comparison, the incidence rate in any dosed group was not statistically significantly greater than that of the vehicle control group. Notably, the 10% incidence of hemangioma and malignant hemangiosarcoma combined at 750 mg/kg b.i.d. was within the historical background range of 0-12%. The high-dose level of 750 mg/kg/day arimoclomol, in the female and male mice have corresponding AUC0-24 of 46100 ng•h/mL (Week 26), and AUC0-24 of 56000 ng•h/mL (Week 26), respectively. Sex differences in arimoclomol Cmax and AUC0-10h values were less than 2-fold. Exposure, as assessed by arimoclomol citrate Cmax and AUC0-10h values, increased with the increase in dose from 100 to 750 mg/kg b.i.d. The increases in Cmax and AUC0-10h values were generally dose proportional. No accumulation of arimoclomol citrate was observed after multiple doses in mice. Mouse Study Comments: Arimoclomol did not affect the overall survival rate up to high dose of 750 mg/kg/day in males and females. The survival rates were 97%, 100%, 93% and 100% for males, and 97%, 97%, 93% and 93% for females, in the dose groups 0 (vehicle), 200, 550 and 1500 mg/kg/day, respectively, and 100% and 90% for males and females, respectively, for the positive control group. Abbreviations: Arim, arimoclomol; NPC1, Niemann-Pick disease Type C 1 gene variant. A clear phenotype-genotype correlation is not well described for most pathogenic variants in NPC1. And the current understanding is that alleles may be best understood in the context of how the predicted abnormal protein variant is able to be processed, localized, and trafficked compared to the wild type protein (Shammas et al. 2019), as this intracellular location may rely on both folding of the protein and post-translational modification. However, compound heterozygosity for different alleles also appears to modify intracellular expression of NPC1. This literature suggests that genotype alone may not be sufficient enough to predict disease severity and that additional studies describing the intracellular localization and mechanistic impact of the affected NPC1 protein are also important to predict clinical phenotype. Review of the genotype data showed an imbalance of functional null molecular variants, in the arimoclomol arm, with three patients in the arimoclomol arm of Study NPC-002 noted to have double null molecular variants (Table 98) compared to none in the placebo arm. Shea, Vice President, Regulatory Affairs Debleena Sengupta, Director Regulatory Affairs Otsuka Bob McQuade, Executive Vice President, Chief Strategic Officer Charlotte Jones-Burton, Vice President, Global Clinical Development, Nephrology Michael Fahmy, Sr. Director, Global Regulatory Affairs Catherine Sheppard, Director, Global Regulatory Affairs 1.0 BACKGROUND Vadadustat is a synthetic, orally bioavailable, small molecule that inhibits hypoxia- inducible factor (HIF) prolyl-hydroxylase (PH) enzymes, leading to stabilization and increased levels of hypoxia inducible-factor alpha, resulting in stimulation of erythropoietin (EPO) expression and improved production of Hb and red blood cells (RBCs). Based on the proposed mechanism of action, a research and development program was opened under IND 102465 in 2009 and trials were conducted to characterize the safety and efficacy of oral vadadustat tablets to treat anemia associated with chronic kidney disease (CKD), in patients on and not on dialysis. There have been 20 completed phase 1 studies (including 1 regional Japanese study), 8 completed phase 2 studies (including 2 regional Japanese studies), and 8 completed phase 3 studies (4 pivotal global phase 3 and 4 supportive regional Japanese phase 3 studies). There are 2 ongoing/planned phase 3b studies that evaluate different vadadustat dosing regimen in patients on dialysis. Vadadustat has been studied for the treatment of anemia associated with CKD including in 4 global phase 3 studies. The global phase 3 studies include two studies in adult subjects with anemia associated with NDD-CKD (PRO2TECT Studies: AKB-6548-CI-0014 and AKB-6548-CI-0015) and 2 studies in adult subjects with anemia associated with DD-CKD (INNO2VATE Studies: AKB-6548-CI-0016 and AKB-6548-CI- 0017). All 4 studies were multi-center/multi-nationals, randomized, open-label, sponsor- blinded, active-controlled (darbepoetin alfa), non-inferiority efficacy and safety CV outcome studies. The primary endpoint for efficacy was mean change in Hb between Baseline and Weeks 24 to 36. The primary safety endpoint assessed major adverse cardiovascular event (MACE) parameters (defined as death, non-fatal MI and non-fatal stroke), specifically as time to first MACE, which was used in sample size determination Reference ID: 4698417

IND 102465 Page 3 U.S. Food and Drug Administration Silver Spring, MD 20993 www.fda.gov for each of the programs. Each study had a vadadustat starting dose of 300 mg once- daily with the opportunity to dose titrate from 150 to 600 mg once-daily to reach and maintain Hb at the targeted range (10-11 g/dL in US and 10-12 g/dL Ex-US). The Hb target ranges for US and Ex-US were established based on FDA and European Medicines Agency’s (EMA’s) guidance to follow Hb targets established in the US Prescribing Information (PI) and Summary of Product Characteristics (SmPC) for ESAs, respectively. Study duration was 36 weeks, with the opportunity to continue on long- term treatment until trial completion. The purpose of the meeting is to provide a preview of the proposed structure and content of the planned NDA in advance of the NDA submission and an overview of the data from the global phase 3 studies. The expected outcomes of the meeting are to: • Reach agreement that the global phase 3 studies are sufficient to support NDA Filing for the target indication in the US • Reach agreement on a select topic for CMC for the planned NDA • Review and reach agreement on the structure and content of the planned NDA • Reach agreement that the clinical pharmacology program supports NDA filing • Reach agreement that a Pregnancy Exposure Registry is not required • Reach agreement on the proposed dates and content for the 120-day safety update • Align on Akebia’s approach for regulatory administrative information inclusion in the NDA FDA sent Preliminary Comments to Akebia Therapeutics on October 20, 2020. 2.0 DISCUSSION FDA Preamble: To evaluate the risk of cardiovascular AEs associated with vadadustat administration, a safety endpoint was defined for both the PRO2TECT program and the INNO2VATE program, as time to first MACE. Akebia powered its pivotal trial programs, in relation to both duration of treatment and sample size, to reach sufficient number of MACE per program, which was deemed adequate to provide statistical support to any non-inferiority conclusions resulting from the pivotal trials. In addition, there was agreement that successful demonstration of non-inferiority, in relation to active comparator (i.e. darbepoetin alfa), on both primary efficacy and primary safety endpoints will be necessary for approval for the proposed specific indication. As per summary efficacy results provided in the meeting package, you demonstrated non-inferiority for efficacy for patients with anemia associated with CKD, who were on dialysis and not on dialysis via Hemoglobin (Hb) endpoint. In addition, you demonstrated non-inferiority for the safety MACE endpoint for patients with anemia associated with CKD, who were on dialysis. However, the MACE analysis conducted in the ‘not on dialysis’ population did not demonstrate non-inferiority to darbepoetin. Summary of Regulatory History Eplontersen was developed under investigational new drug (IND) 139521 by Ionis Pharmaceuticals, Inc. (Applicant), in collaboration with Akcea Therapeutics, Inc., for the treatment of the polyneuropathy of hereditary transthyretin (TTR)-mediated amyloidosis (hATTR) in adults. Eplontersen is an antisense oligonucleotide that specifically binds to and leads to degradation of TTR messenger ribonucleic acid, reducing the TTR protein synthesis process. The Applicant initially had a Type B PIND meeting request to receive feedback on their development plans for eplontersen. The meeting occurred on February 21, 2019, and the Applicant’s proposals were discussed. The FDA did not agree with the proposal to use TTR reduction as a primary endpoint for the Phase 3 study but instead, proposed the use of the Norfolk-QOL-DN and mNIS+7 as co-primary endpoints as TTR reduction would be most appropriate as a secondary endpoint, with adjustment for multiplicity. The FDA received IND 139521 for eplontersen (investigational product ION-682844) injection on August 8, 2019. The study was allowed to proceed after the Applicant agreed to amend Study ION-682884-CS3 by changing the safety monitoring plan to follow the paradigm in the Tegsedi USPI. The amended protocol was submitted on October 2, 2019. On March 5, 2021, the Applicant requested a Type C meeting to discuss the suitability of their proposed Phase 1 study (ION-682884-CS21) for demonstrating bioequivalence between a vial, prefilled syringe with safety device, and autoinjector configurations. The Agency provided written responses to the Applicant on May 19, 2021, stating that the proposed clinical study design for ION-682884-CS21 was not adequately designed to demonstrate bioequivalence between the vial, prefilled syringe with safety device, and autoinjector configurations and provided recommendations for the Applicant’s consideration. In addition, the Applicant was advised to conduct a comprehensive use-related risk analysis, which would determine the need to submit a human factors validation study. On April 6, 2021, the Applicant requested a Type C chemistry, manufacturing, and controls meeting to obtain advice from FDA regarding the proposed classification Written responses were provided on June 11, 2021, stating that the final designation will be determined during the new drug application (NDA) review with the completion of the commercial manufacturing process of the drug substance. Eplontersen received orphan drug designation for the treatment of the polyneuropathy of hereditary transthyretin (TTR)-mediated amyloidosis (hATTR) in adults on January 6, 2022. In response to the Applicant’s March 31, 2022, thorough QT (TQT) study waiver request, the QT-IRT team determined that nonclinical assessments could be used as a substitute for a TQT study because the integrated data showed that eplontersen does not cause clinically significant QTc interval prolongation. The Applicant was notified of this determination on August 4, 2022. Pharmacology Eplontersen (ION-682884) is a 20-mer chimeric 2′-MOE mixed (PS/PO) backbone ASO conjugated to GalNAc3 that targets the 3′-UTR of human TTR mRNA to suppress both wild type and mutant TTR transcription. In vitro studies in human hepatocytes indicated an IC50 of 0.059 µM for the suppression of human TTR mRNA by eplontersen. Eplontersen is complimentary to human and monkey, but not rodent, TTR mRNA; therefore, transgenic mice carrying the Ile84Ser human TTR mutant were used to test the pharmacologic effects of eplontersen. Subcutaneous (SC) administration of 0.6-6 mg/kg eplontersen for 3 weeks QW in male human TTR transgenic mice resulted in dose-dependent reductions in hepatic hTTR mRNA levels, with an ED50 of 0.5 mg/kg/week, which corresponded to reductions in plasma hTTR protein, with an ED50 of 1.5 mg/kg/week. 13.1.2. Coprimary Efficacy Endpoint The Applicant also used percent change from baseline in serum TTR protein concentration at week 35 as a primary efficacy endpoint, given the mechanism of action of eplontersen in reducing serum TTR protein levels. The Agency had recommended that the Applicant not utilize serum TTR reduction as a primary endpoint for their Phase 3 study in a pre-IND meeting on February 21, 2019, as stated below: “We do not agree with your proposal to use TTR reduction as a primary endpoint for your Phase 3 study. Although we note the importance of TTR reduction based on the mechanism of the drug, clinical outcomes should be assessed as the primary endpoints for the study. We strongly recommended the use of the Norfolk-QOL-DN and mNIS+7 as coprimary endpoints. TTR reduction would be most appropriate as a secondary endpoint, with adjustment for multiplicity.” For this reason, this clinical review will not refer to percent change from baseline in serum TTR protein concentration as a primary efficacy endpoint and will instead be evaluated as an additional endpoint. Secondary Efficacy Endpoints The secondary efficacy endpoint at the week 35 interim analysis was the change from baseline in the Norfolk QOL-DN at week 35. The Norfolk QoL-DN questionnaire is a standardized 35-item patient-reported outcomes measure that is sensitive to the different features of diabetic neuropathy: small fiber, large fiber, and autonomic nerve function. There are 35 questions divided into 5 domains. The range of possible total scores is -4 to 136. Higher scores indicate a worse quality of life. A negative score is possible because in Question 31, “Very Good” is scored as –1, and “Excellent” is scored as –2. In Question 32, “Somewhat better” is scored as –1 and “Much better” is scored as -2. Findings of hemorrhage in the rats included thymus, mesenteric and submandibular lymph nodes, and bone (femur) in the 4-week study, and bone (femur, tibia, sternum), ovary, and liver in the 3-month study. Finding of hemorrhage in the monkeys included esophagus and colon in the 4-week study and rectum, thyroid, lymph node, and uterus in the 3-month study. Hemorrhage in animals may be secondary to inflammation; however, considering all the nonclinical data, there was no mechanistic rationale for the hemorrhage observed in the clinic. Overall, tovorafenib related adverse findings in animal toxicology studies included: gastrointestinal, epidermal (including skin), hematologic, and hepatotoxicity; pro-inflammatory events leading to findings in the thyroid and parathyroid and changes in levels of hormones, calcium, and phosphorus. Toxicities were observed in reproductive organs in the general toxicology studies and included reversible increased thickness of the vaginal mucosa, increased size and/or numbers of corpora hemorrhagicum, and hemorrhage, and non-reversible cystic follicles, decreased corpora lutea, and interstitial cell hyperplasia in ovaries in female rats, and reduced weights of epididymis and testes, which correlated with reversible tubular degeneration/atrophy of the testes and reduced epididymal sperm in male rats. Tovorafenib was negative for genotoxicity in the following studies: in vitro bacterial reverse mutation (Ames) assay, in vitro micronucleus assay in human lymphocytes, and in vivo bone marrow micronucleus assay in rats. Tovorafenib was positive in the in vitro chromosomal aberration assay; this occurred at a single concentration that was associated with drug precipitation. Because of the potential for prolonged treatment and long-term survival in the proposed patient population, it is important to address the carcinogenicity potential of tovorafenib. Two post-marketing requirements (PMRs) to conduct carcinogenicity studies in mice and rats were communicated to the Applicant. Of note, the Applicant submitted a special protocol assessment for a on July 7, 2023, under IND 108340 for DAY101. A preliminary GLP-compliant dose range-finding embryo-fetal development study was conducted in pregnant rats to assess the effect of tovorafenib on fetal development. Once daily oral dosing for 12 days, between gestation days (GD) 7 and 17 during the period of organogenesis, resulted in total litter loss at the lowest dose of ≥37.5 mg/kg/day which is approximately 0.8 times the recommended clinical dose of 380 mg/m2 once weekly based on AUC. Treated dams had no clinical signs at doses as high as 150 mg/kg/day. Due to the discernable embryofetal toxicity signal, the FDA agreed that an additional study was not likely warranted. A GLP-compliant fertility and early embryonic development study was conducted in male and female rats to assess the effect of tovorafenib on fertility and embryonic development parameters. Once daily oral administration of tovorafenib in rats at doses of 37.5, 75, or 150 mg/kg/day for 64 days beginning 29 days before mating had no effect on male reproductive success (mating) or fertility parameters (sperm density, or sperm motility). However, females administered the same doses for 14 days prior to cohabitation through GD 6 demonstrated significantly impaired reproductive and fertility parameters at the same dose Reference ID: 5368881 (b) (4)

Director Clinical Pharmacology Joseph Truitt President & Chief Executive Officer 1.0 BACKGROUND Danicopan, formerly ACH-0144471, is a small molecule, orally administered, factor D (FD) inhibitor, is in development by Achillion Pharmaceuticals, Inc. for the treatment of complement-mediated diseases, such as paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) and C3 glomerulopathy (C3G). Factor D is a serine protease that catalyzes the cleavage of factor B, a rate-limiting step in the alternative pathway (AP) of complement. By inhibiting FD, danicopan potently and specifically inhibits AP activity. Interim data from a Phase 2 proof-of-concept study (ACH471-101) has demonstrated the efficacy of danicopan, in addition to standard of care eculizumab, a C5 inhibitor, at stable dose and regimen, by increasing hemoglobin levels after 24 weeks of treatment in PNH patients. Results from this ongoing Phase 2 combination study continue to demonstrate clinically significant improvements in both the primary and secondary endpoints. A mean increase in hemoglobin ≥ 2 g/dL was demonstrated, from a mean of 7.9 g/dL. This treatment benefit appears by Week 2 of treatment with danicopan for most patients Achillion Pharmaceuticals, Inc. requested a type B meeting with the FDA on August 7, 2019, to discuss the existing data and to align on a proposed single, global Phase 3 study to support a future NDA submission. FDA sent Preliminary Comments to Achillion Pharmaceuticals, Inc. on October 21, 2019. 2. DISCUSSION 2.1. Questions Question 1: Does the Division agree that the clinical pharmacology of danicopan has been adequately characterized and that the program (once complete) is sufficient to support an NDA? FDA Response to Question 1: Yes, the overall approach is reasonable. However, the completeness and acceptability of data will be a review issue. Reference ID: 4519959 (b) (4) (b) (4)

Discussion: The FDA clarified that the approach was reasonable and stated that if any additional information was needed by the QT/IRT, the sponsor will be notified. Question 2: Does the Division agree with the current population as defined by the inclusion exclusion criteria in the proposed Phase 3 study in combination with an approved C5 inhibitor (Study ACH471-105)? FDA Response to Question 2: No, the single-arm trial add-on trial design will not allow for isolation of the treatment effect of the addition of your agent to the C5 inhibitor. We recommend that you consider conducting randomized controlled trials in patients with PNH who have residual anemia despite anti-C5 therapy for at least 6 months. Two potential trial options for this population include: an add-on trial design (danicopan plus C5 inhibitor versus continuation of C5 inhibitor alone) or randomized controlled trial design of danicopan monotherapy versus continued anti-C5 inhibitor. In addition, we have the following concerns and considerations regarding the design of the proposed Phase 3 study.  The proposed enrollment criterion of hemoglobin may not adequately represent a patient population that requires therapy. You should consider a lower hemoglobin concentration (e.g. < 9 g/dL) enrollment criterion to better define a patient population that requires therapy. Also, consider incorporating an entry criterion for a specified minimum red blood cell transfusion requirement.  It is not clear that the proposed primary endpoint, i.e. increase in hemoglobin relative to baseline at week 24 (mean change of 1.5 g/dL) will permit a demonstration of sufficient magnitude of change or meaningful clinical benefit. Discuss evaluating an increase of hemoglobin ≥ 2g/dL in absence of transfusion or other PNH therapy and maintained during the last 12 weeks of study treatment of the 6 month treatment period.  Demonstration of change in meaningful clinical benefit such as transfusion avoidance will be critical. IND 127367 Page 4 U.S. Food and Drug Administration Silver Spring, MD 20993 www.fda.gov 3.0 OTHER MEETING INFORMATION PREA REQUIREMENTS Under the Pediatric Research Equity Act (PREA) (codified at section 505B of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act), 21 U.S.C. 355c), all applications for new active ingredients (which includes new salts and new fixed combinations), new indications, new dosage forms, new dosing regimens, or new routes of administration are required to contain an assessment of the safety and effectiveness of the product for the claimed indication(s) in pediatric patients unless this requirement is waived or deferred (see section 505B(a)(1)(A) of the FD&C Act). Applications for drugs or biological products for which orphan designation has been granted that otherwise would be subject to the requirements of section 505B(a)(1)(A) are exempt pursuant to section 505B(k)(1) from the PREA requirement to conduct pediatric assessments. Title V of the FDA Reauthorization Act of 2017 (FDARA) amended the statute to create section 505B(a)(1)(B), which requires that any original marketing application for certain adult oncology drugs (i.e., those intended for treatment of an adult cancer and with molecular targets that FDA has determined to be substantially relevant to the growth or progression of a pediatric cancer) that are submitted on or after August 18, 2020, contain reports of molecularly targeted pediatric cancer investigations. See link to list of relevant molecular targets below. These molecularly targeted pediatric cancer investigations must be “designed to yield clinically meaningful pediatric study data, gathered using appropriate formulations for each age group for which the study is required, regarding dosing, safety, and preliminary efficacy to inform potential pediatric labeling” (section 505B(a)(3)). Applications for drugs or biological products for which orphan designation has been granted and which are subject to the requirements of section 505B(a)(1)(B), however, will not be exempt from PREA (see section 505B(k)(2)) and will be required to include plans to conduct the molecularly targeted pediatric investigations as required, unless such investigations are waived or deferred. Under section 505B(e)(2)(A)(i) of the FD&C Act, you must submit an Initial Pediatric Study Plan (iPSP) within 60 days of an End of Phase 2 (EOP2) meeting, or such other time as agreed upon with FDA. IND 140832 Page 2 Sarah Labriola, M.S. Manager, Regulatory Affairs Jacqueline Cinicola, M.S. Senior Director, Regulatory Affairs Kha Le, Ph.D. Director, Clinical Pharmacology BACKGROUND Regulatory On April 20, 2015, Agios Pharmaceuticals, Inc. (Agios) submitted an Investigational New Drug (IND) application including Protocol AG881-C-002, entitled “A Phase 1, Multicenter, Open- Label, Dose-Escalation and Expansion, Safety, Pharmacokinetic, Pharmacodynamic, and Clinical Activity Study of Orally Administered AG-881 in Patients with Advanced Solid Tumors, Including Gliomas, with an IDH1 and/or IDH2 Mutation.” Protocol AG881-C-002 was initiated under IND 124865 with the Division of Hematology Products (DHP). The IND went to effect on April 20, 2015. On July 25, 2018, DHP recommended that Agios submit a new IND to the Division of Oncology Products 2 (DOP2) for AG-881 for the treatment of advanced solid tumors, including glioma, that harbor an isocitrate dehydrogenase-1 (IDH1) and/or isocitrate dehydrogenase-2 (IDH2) mutation, since Protocol AG881-C-002 included a glioma component with over 40 patients. On September 10, 2018, vorasidenib (AG-881) was granted orphan drug designation for the treatment of patients with glioma that harbors an IDH mutation. On September 24, 2018, Agios submitted IND 140832, including Protocol AG881-C-002. As Protocol AG881-C-002 had already completed enrollment, Agios submitted a request to waive the 30-day review period for IND 140832. The 30-day review period waiver was granted on October 1, 2018. On January 25, 2019, Agios requested a Type B, End-of-Phase 2 meeting with DOP2 to obtain input on the design of a study with AG-881 for the treatment of patients with grade 2 glioma harboring an IDH1or IDH2 mutation who have undergone surgery as their only treatment. The results of the trial, if positive, are intended to support a New Drug Application (NDA) filing. Agios is seeking agreement and advice on the proposed protocol design, including volumetric tumor growth rate as a novel primary endpoint. Agios notes that separate interactions will be sought to specifically discuss their patient-reported outcome measurement strategy for the planned study and the pharmacologic development of AG-881. The meeting was granted on February 6, 2019, and the meeting package was received on February 15, 2019. Nonclinical AG-881 is a central nervous system (CNS)-penetrant, small molecule inhibitor of mutant IDH1 and IDH2 proteins. Agios has conducted several in vitro and in vivo pharmacology studies, cardiovascular and CNS safety pharmacology studies, good laboratory practice (GLP)-compliant 28-day repeat-dose toxicology studies in Sprague-Dawley (SD) rats and cynomolgus monkeys, a GLP ototoxicity study in SD rats, and genotoxicity assessments. Reference ID: 4419209

IND 140832 Page 3 FDA (in a March 23, 2018 emailed response to a March 19, 2018 emailed inquiry from Agios, under parent IND 124865) stated that the intended patient population of patients with low grade gliomas (LGG) harboring IDH1 or IDH2 mutations who have previously undergone surgical resection appears to fall within the scope of ICH S9; therefore, 3 months is an appropriate duration for the chronic toxicology studies. Agios stated they plan to submit the results of the 3- month GLP toxicology studies in SD rats and cynomolgus monkeys prior to initiation of the proposed Phase 3 trial. Agios also stated that they plan to conduct an in vitro GLP BALB/c 3T3 mouse fibroblast assay, GLP dose range-finding and definitive embryo-fetal development studies in SD rats and New Zealand White rabbits, and a GLP in vivo micronucleus assay in SD rats. Clinical Disease Background Gliomas account for 30 to 40% of all intracranial tumors and are the second most common form of primary brain tumors. Low-grade gliomas (LGG) or grade 2 gliomas comprising the oligodendroglial and astrocytic subtypes are rare with approximately 3500 new cases occurring annually. Mutations in IDH occur in the majority of LGG and are considered driver mutations associated with altered cellular metabolism and activation of the hypoxia pathway. IDH mutation-positive gliomas are slower growing, tend to be diagnosed in younger patients, and are associated with the hypermethylation phenotype, which carries a more favorable prognosis compared to gliomas with wild-type IDH. Although the median survival of IDH mutation- positive LGG may range from a few years to decades, most tumors will accumulate additional genetic mutations and eventually evolve to higher grade disease. Agios states that the optimal treatment regimen for patients with IDH mutant LGG has not been well defined. Beyond standard of care surgical resection, treatment approaches in LGG vary with the goal to delay toxicities secondary to chemotherapy and radiation therapy. Currently there are no approved therapies for LGG, and systemic therapy has been adapted based on approved therapies in anaplastic astrocytoma and glioblastoma. Agios reports that observation remains an option in the current treatment guidelines for LGG. In recurrent LGG, treatment options include repeat surgery, chemoradiation if not pursued initially, re-irradiation, and chemotherapy alone. Clinical Development Agios reports that AG-881 is being studied in the ongoing first-in-human, open-label, single- arm, dose escalation and expansion study AG881-C-002, designed to evaluate the safety and tolerability of AG-881 as a single agent when administered orally once daily (QD) in 28-day cycles to patients with solid tumors with an IDH1 and/or IDH2 mutation. The primary objectives of this trial are to determine the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) and/or the recommended Phase 2 dose (RP2D) of AG-881 in patients with advanced solid tumors including glioma. The secondary objectives of this study are to characterize the pharmacokinetics (PK), pharmacodynamics (PD), and preliminary clinical activity of AG-881 in patients with solid tumors. Additionally, an exploratory objective is to assess changes in tumor volume growth rate in patients with non-enhancing glioma based on tumor volume measurements from serial MRI Reference ID: 4419209

IND 140832 Page 4 exams (FLAIR or T2 sequences) or to determine if change in tumor growth rate before and after treatment is associated with progression as assessed by Response Assessment in Neuro-oncology LGG (RANO-LGG). Study enrollment completed in June 2017. A total of 93 patients enrolled, including 52 patients with glioma (30 patients with enhancing disease and 22 patients with non-enhancing disease as assessed by the investigator). Five dose levels of AG-881, ranging from 25 mg to 300 mg QD, were initially tested in patients with glioma. Transaminase elevation was observed as a common adverse event (approximately 40%, all grades) with the majority being grade 1 or 2 events. Five adverse events (AEs) of grade 2 or higher transaminase elevation in patients receiving a dose of 100 mg QD or higher were determined to be dose limiting toxicities (DLTs). All five events were reversible to grade ≤1 with dose modification or discontinuation. Although the MTD was not reached, the decision was made to proceed with study of dose levels less than 100 mg QD in glioma. As of the July 20, 2018, data cutoff, all glioma patients had experienced at least one treatment- emergent AE (TEAE) and ten (9.2%) had experienced a grade 3 or higher AE. The following TEAEs occurred in ≥20% of patients: alanine aminotransferase (ALT) or aspartate aminotransferase (AST) elevation, headache, fatigue, nausea and seizure. As of the data cutoff, 14 (26.9%) of the 52 patients remained on treatment; these included 13 patients with non- enhancing glioma. Of the 28 patients who discontinued treatment, 29 (76.3%) discontinued due to disease progression and 2 (5.2%) discontinued due to elevated transaminases. The median treatment duration for patients with non-enhancing disease is 15 months (range 1-32 months) and the median treatment duration for patients with enhancing disease is 3.25 months (range 0.2-3 months). All 52 patients were evaluated for clinical efficacy as of the July 20, 2018, data cutoff. Patients with non-enhancing disease were assessed using the updated RANO-LGG criteria and those with enhancing disease were assessed using the original RANO criteria. Agios reports that the preliminary clinical activity in the glioma population was greater in patients with non-enhancing tumor as compared to patients with enhancing tumor. According to the investigator’s assessment of non-enhancing glioma patients, 9% (n=2) had a confirmed response (one partial response and one minor response) and an additional 81% had stable disease. No patients with enhancing glioma demonstrated a response. Clinical Disease Background Gliomas account for 30 to 40% of all intracranial tumors and are the second most common form of primary brain tumors. Low-grade gliomas (LGG) or grade 2 gliomas comprising the oligodendroglial and astrocytic subtypes are rare with approximately 3500 new cases occurring annually. Mutations in IDH occur in the majority of LGG and are considered driver mutations associated with altered cellular metabolism and activation of the hypoxia pathway. IDH mutation-positive gliomas are slower growing, tend to be diagnosed in younger patients, and are associated with the hypermethylation phenotype, which carries a more favorable prognosis compared to gliomas with wild-type IDH. Although the median survival of IDH mutation- positive LGG may range from a few years to decades, most tumors will accumulate additional genetic mutations and eventually evolve to higher grade disease. Agios states that the optimal treatment regimen for patients with IDH mutant LGG has not been well defined. Beyond standard of care surgical resection, treatment approaches in LGG vary with the goal to delay toxicities secondary to chemotherapy and radiation therapy. Currently there are no approved therapies for LGG, and systemic therapy has been adapted based on approved therapies in anaplastic astrocytoma and glioblastoma. Agios reports that observation remains an option in the current treatment guidelines for LGG. In recurrent LGG, treatment options include repeat surgery, chemoradiation if not pursued initially, re-irradiation, and chemotherapy alone. Although the MTD was not reached, the decision was made to proceed with study of dose levels less than 100 mg QD in glioma. As of the July 20, 2018, data cutoff, all glioma patients had experienced at least one treatment- emergent AE (TEAE) and ten (9.2%) had experienced a grade 3 or higher AE. IND 140832 Page 3 U.S. Food and Drug Administration Silver Spring, MD 20993 www.fda.gov FDA sent Preliminary Comments to Servier on September 7, 2023. Regulatory Vorasidenib was granted an orphan drug designation (2018-6493) for treatment of patients with glioma that harbor an IDH mutation. In March 2023, fast track approval was granted based on the objective response rate (ORR) in studies AG120-881-C-001 and AG881-C-002. In June 2023, breakthrough therapy designation was granted based on a clinically and statistically significant improvement in progression free survival (PFS) in the vorasidenib arm compared with placebo determined by a blinded independent review committee (BIRC) in the INDIGO study. Nonclinical Vorasidenib is a small molecule inhibitor of mutant isocitrate dehydrogenase 1 and 2 (IDH1 and IDH2) proteins. The nonclinical package includes in vitro and in vivo pharmacology studies, including proof-of-concept studies; in vitro and in vivo pharmacokinetic (PK) studies; safety pharmacology studies for central nervous system and cardiovascular assessments, GLP-compliant repeat-dose toxicology studies up to 13 weeks’ duration in Sprague-Dawley (SD) rats and cynomolgus monkeys, a GLP- compliant 28-day ototoxicity study in SD rats, genotoxicity and phototoxicity assessments, and embryo-fetal development toxicity studies in rats and rabbits. The nonclinical studies were conducted under parent IND 124865. Clinical Study AG881-C-004 is a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of vorasidenib in patients with residual or recurrent grade 2 glioma with an IDH1 or IDH2 mutation. The primary endpoint is radiographic PFS by modified Response Assessment in Neuro-oncology-Low Grade Glioma (RANO-LGG) criteria per blinded independent review committee (BIRC). The study includes patients with residual or recurrent predominantly non-enhancing Grade 2 oligodendroglioma or astrocytoma with an IDH1 or IDH2 mutation, who have undergone surgery as their only treatment. There are no approved first line therapies specifically for patients with IDH mutations. NCCN guidelines for low-risk, grade 2, IDH-mutant LGG include observation or clinical trials with a goal to delay utilization of toxic therapies. For patients with recurrent disease observation after re-resection, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, or targeted therapy (ivosidenib) are options. At the time of the planned interim analysis 2 (IA2) with 82% information fraction (135 PFS events of the 164 PFS events planned at the final analysis), PFS by BIRC was Reference ID: 5253334

IND 140832 Page 4 U.S. Food and Drug Administration Silver Spring, MD 20993 www.fda.gov statistically significant in the vorasidenib arm (40 mg orally daily) compared with placebo (HR=0.39, 95% CI, 0.27 to 0.56, P=0.000000067) and the median PFS by BIRC for patients randomized to vorasidenib was 27.7 months versus 11.1 months for patients randomized to placebo. The study also met its key secondary endpoint at the time of IA2; TTNI, was determined to be statistically significantly improved in the vorasidenib arm compared with placebo with a HR=0.26. Following the recommendation of an Independent Data Monitoring Committee (IDMC) upon review of this data, the study was unblinded in March 2023 due to early demonstration of efficacy. Serious adverse events (SAEs) that occurred in ≥ 2 patients who received vorasidenib without crossover were: seizure (6 [3.5%] patients) and ALT increased (2 [1.2%] patients). The most common treatment emergent AEs with a > 5% difference in incidence between the vorasidenib and placebo arms were hepatic-related events, largely lab abnormalities, and diarrhea; events were largely Grade 1 and Grade 2, though three of the SAEs reported in one patient each on the vorasidenib arm were events of autoimmune hepatitis, hepatic failure, and ALT increased. Supportive studies:  Study AG120-881-C-001 is a multicenter, randomized, controlled, open-label, perioperative study of ivosidenib or vorasidenib in patients with recurrent, non- enhancing, IDH1 mutant, low-grade glioma (n= 24). Preliminary clinical activity data are available for all 24 patients including 14 who received 50 mg daily. Among patients who received 50 mg daily, two patients (14%) had a partial response and four patients (29%) had a minor response.  Study AG881-C-001 was a multicenter, open-label, dose-escalation safety, PK, pharmacodynamic (PD), and clinical activity study of orally administered vorasidenib in patients with advanced hematologic malignancies with an IDH1 and/or IDH2 mutation. For the AML subgroup, the ORR (including CR, complete remission with incomplete platelet recovery/complete remission with incomplete hematologic recovery, partial remission, and morphologic leukemia-free state) was 5.9% (95% CI: 0.7%, 19.7%). For the MDS subgroup, the ORR (including CR, marrow CR, and partial remission) was 36.4% (95% CI: 10.9 to 69.2).  Study AG881-C-002 is a multicenter, open-label, dose-escalation and expansion, safety, PK, PD, and clinical activity study of orally administered vorasidenib (at 50 mg daily, n=11) in patients with gliomas with an IDH1 and/or IDH2 mutation (n=52). For patients with non-enhancing glioma (n = 22), one patient (4.5%) had a partial response and three patients (14%) had a minor response. Response durations ranged from 7.4 – 27.7 months. The sponsor reported a median PFS of 36.8 months in patients with non-enhancing disease. Based on these data, the Sponsor is planning to submit an NDA for the proposed indication. Reference ID: 5253334

Preliminary clinical activity data are available for all 24 patients including 14 who received 50 mg daily. Among patients who received 50 mg daily, two patients (14%) had a partial response and four patients (29%) had a minor response.  Study AG881-C-001 was a multicenter, open-label, dose-escalation safety, PK, pharmacodynamic (PD), and clinical activity study of orally administered vorasidenib in patients with advanced hematologic malignancies with an IDH1 and/or IDH2 mutation. For the MDS subgroup, the ORR (including CR, marrow CR, and partial remission) was 36.4% (95% CI: 10.9 to 69.2).  Study AG881-C-002 is a multicenter, open-label, dose-escalation and expansion, safety, PK, PD, and clinical activity study of orally administered vorasidenib (at 50 mg daily, n=11) in patients with gliomas with an IDH1 and/or IDH2 mutation (n=52). provenancePages.text: NDA 219132 Aqneursa (levacetylleucine) 131 Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23) The following study was previously reviewed under the IND: Study Number 36243: 6-Week Subchronic Toxicity Study of IB1001 by Repeated Oral Administration to Beagle Dogs Purpose: Evaluate oral toxicity following daily dosing and reversibility of effects in dogs. Design: Daily oral dosing in Beagle dogs (3M/3F per dose level + 2M/2F in the high dose and control groups) dosed at 0, 225, 750, or 2500 mg/kg/day for 6 weeks followed by a recovery period of 2 weeks. Body weight, feed consumption, electrocardiography (ECG), blood pressure, ophthalmological and auditory examinations, clinical pathology, histopathology, and toxicokinetics (TKs) were evaluated. Key Findings: There were no adverse effects at up to 2500 mg/kg/day. The maximum plasma concentration (Cmax) and area under the concentration-time curve (AUC) levels of levacetylleucine were dose-related after Days 1 and 42 of dosing. The combined male and female Cmax was 252.8 µg/mL and AUC0-∞ was 598 µg.hr/mL at the no-observed-adverse- effect level (NOAEL) on Day 42. Conclusion: The NOAEL for levacetylleucine was 2500 mg/kg/day in a 6-week oral gavage toxicity study in Beagle dogs. The NOAEL dose in dog provides a 19-fold safety margin based on exposures in humans (31.6 µg·hr/mL) at a daily maximum recommended human dose of 4 g/day. 13.2. Individual Reviews of Studies Submitted With the New Drug Application 13.2.1. Nonclinical Pharmacodynamic Data Data to support the mechanism of action for levacetylleucine were derived from published literature. The Applicant described data suggesting that in cultured Chinese hamster ovary cells, treatment with levacetylleucine at a concentration of 1mM for 24 hours, was associated with a modest reduction in lysosomal volume, sphingosine, glycosphingolipids (GSLs), and a very modest reduction in stored cholesterol. In NPC patient-derived fibroblasts, treatment with levacetylleucine was also associated with a modest reduction in apparent lysosomal volume when cells were cultured for 7 days with 1mM levacetylleucine (Mann 2018). These studies suggest that levacetylleucine has the potential to reduce stored intracellular lipid; however, the mechanism of action for this drug, including the molecular targets by which it elicits these effects, is unclear. The Applicant also provided published data from an animal disease model. In Npc1-/- mice, pre-symptomatic (from the age of 3 weeks old) treatment with levacetylleucine was also associated with a modest increase in survival and a reduction in markers of neuroinflammation (CD68 staining) in the cerebellum (Section 13.2.2; (Kaya et al. 2021). The above changes were not monitored in the clinical trial to evaluate the association of change in magnitude of levels of GSL and neuroinflammation with the dose of levacetylleucine and efficacy. At the Division’s request, the Applicant provided raw data obtained by the publication’s authors, and a letter of reference granting them the right to use the raw data (submission dated July 3, 2024) and revised right to use raw data certifying that spreadsheets accurately reflect the data contained in publication by Kaya et al. 2021. Summary of Regulatory History The Applicant, IntraBio Inc, has investigated levacetylleucine, also referred to by the company development code IB1001 and by its chemical name N-acetyl-L-leucine (NALL), for its ability to treat Niemann-Pick disease type C (NPC). The Applicant’s development program began with the investigation of commercially available racemic mixture N-acetyl- DL-leucine, a modified amino acid approved in France since 1957 as Tanganil (Pierre Fabre Laboratories) for short term (10 days to 6 weeks) treatment of acute vertigo in adults. The Applicant opened a pre-investigational new drug application (PIND) file (PIND 134369) and submitted a PIND meeting request on February 22, 2017, to discuss their development program for N-acetyl-DL-leucine. The meeting was granted by the Agency; however, the Applicant cancelled the meeting on April 13, 2017 because it determined the program needed additional refinement before any discussions should occur. The Applicant also received an orphan drug designation for N-acetyl-DL-leucine for the treatment of NPC on February 22, 2018. The Applicant resubmitted a PIND meeting request on February 26, 2018, this time to discuss their nonclinical and clinical plan to develop levacetylleucine, the L-enantiomer and active ingredient of the racemic mixture of N-acetyl-DL-leucine. The Applicant asserted that animal studies suggested that the L-enantiomer had a greater potential clinical benefit over the racemic mixture. The Applicant intended to formulate levacetylleucine as granules for oral suspension for the treatment of NPC In the PIND meeting, held on July 17, 2018, the FDA commented on the Applicant’s proposed plan to conduct a phase 2/2b, open-label clinical trial to assess the safety and efficacy of levacetylleucine. The FDA asserted that an open-label trial could be used for proof-of-concept, but that it would be inadequate to generate interpretable efficacy data to support a future marketing application. General comments were also provided, particularly for nonclinical studies, primary endpoints considerations, the statistical analysis approach, and the clinical pharmacology development plan. In addition, the FDA advised the Applicant The meeting minutes were issued on July 26, 2018. On January 7, 2019, IND 134369 was submitted and included protocol IB1001-201 titled “Effects of N-Acetyl-L-Leucine on Niemann-Pick Disease Type C: A Multinational, Multicenter, Open-Label, Rater-Blinded Phase II Study.” Per the FDA’s request, a teleconference took place on January 23, 2019. In the teleconference, the FDA reiterated the concerns regarding the limitations of an open-label trial design versus a randomized, controlled trial and reminded the Applicant that Trial IB1001-201, as designed, would only provide short term safety information. The Sponsor acknowledged the FDA’s concerns and stated that Trial IB101-201 was an exploratory study and agreed to revise the protocol per FDA’s recommendation to eliminate the open-label extension and limit the trial to 6 weeks in duration. The FDA issued a Study May Proceed letter on February 7, 2019. The FDA recommended the Applicant request a guidance meeting to discuss improving the trial design (e.g., incorporating randomization) and to further discuss some of the trial’s key elements (e.g., the clinical outcome assessment endpoints and statistical approach). General Reference ID: 5451862 (b) (4) (b) (4) (b) (4)
