With HAE1 the C1-INH levels are low or absent and there is reduced functional activity; with HAE2 the C1-INH levels are normal (or near normal) but there is still significantly reduced functional activity.1 Both types of HAE result in overproduction of the inflammatory peptide bradykinin, leading to vasodilation and swelling.2 The clinical presentation for both HAE1 and HAE2 is the same. Patients present with unpredictable, recurrent, painful, and often debilitating swelling episodes referred to as attacks, which affect subcutaneous tissue (face, upper or lower extremities, genitals), abdominal organs (stomach, intestines, bladder), and the upper airway (larynx, tongue).3 Untreated, swelling typically resolves within two to five days, however in some patients laryngeal angioedema may cause fatal asphyxiation. The written responses for this meeting were issued to and PIND 143698 on April 14, 2021, and provided Agency’s comments on the overall development of sepiapterin for PKU indications, including what would be necessary for marketing application(s) to be submitted via the 505(b)(1) regulatory pathway. On May 28, 2021, the Agency issued type C written responses to PIND 143698 providing comments and seeking clarification on PTC’s proposed use of dried blood sampling via volumetric absorptive micro sampling (VAMS) technology in their proposed phase 3 study. On June 15, 2021, PTC received a rare pediatric disease designation for sepiapterin for the treatment of HPA in patients with PKU. PTC submitted IND 143698 on August 24, 2021, for sepiapterin for the treatment of HPA in patients with PKU. The IND contained a phase 3 protocol, PKU-003 titled “A Phase 3 Study of PTC923 in Subjects with Phenylketonuria,” and a protocol for an OLE Trial, PKU-004 titled “A Phase 3 Open-Label Extension Study of PTC923 in Phenylketonuria.” Included with the IND submission was a request for a Fast Track designation, which was denied on September 22, 2021, because the submitted data were not adequate to support the potential to address an unmet medical need in the context of available therapies for PKU. On September 23, 2021, a partial clinical hold was imposed on protocol PKU-003 to prevent the treatment of patients aged 0 to ≤17 years due to insufficient information to assess the risks to participants (per 21 CFR 312.42(b)(2)(i)) because of a lack of clinical and nonclinical data to support the proposed dosing in those participants. A type A meeting was requested to discuss the partial clinical hold and, in preliminary comments issued on November 5, 2021, the Agency stated that the information that had been provided in the background package for the meeting would be considered adequate to support the treatment of pediatric patients at the proposed doses and that no additional nonclinical studies would be required. PTC subsequently cancelled the meeting because the information provided in the preliminary comments was deemed adequate and submitted their complete response to the clinical hold on December 8, 2021, which included revised protocols (versions 3.0) incorporating FDA recommend changes for PKU-003 and PKU- 004. The partial clinical hold was removed by the Agency on January 6, 2022. PTC subsequently submitted amended protocols (versions 4.0) for PKU-003 and PKU-004 on February 11, 2022, to incorporate additional Agency feedback and to update blood sample volumes. On June 28, 2022, PTC again amended protocol PKU-003 (version 5.0) to add additional blood plasma sampling collection points. A Drug Abuse Liability Assessment for sepiapterin was provided to the Agency on April 25, 2022, and following its review, the Agency informed PTC on December 12, 2022, that no further studies were warranted to evaluate its abuse potential. NDA 219666 SEPHIENCE (sepiapterin) 134 Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23) PTC submitted additional clinical protocols to IND 143698. On July 15, 2022, protocol PTC923- DDI-101-HV, titled “A Phase 1 Study to Evaluate the Potential Effect of PTC923 on BCRP in Healthy Subjects,” was submitted. This trial intended to determine the drug-drug interaction effects of curcumin, an inhibitor of the efflux transporter BCRP, on the PK of sepiapterin and BH4, as well as the effect of sepiapterin on the PK of rosuvastatin, a BCRP substrate. On August 15, 2022, protocol PKU-008, titled “A Phase 1 Study to Investigate the Absorption, Metabolism, and Excretion of 14C-PTC923 Following a Single Oral Dose Administration in Healthy Male Volunteers,” was submitted. On October 26, 2022, PTC submitted a request for a pre- and post-natal developmental study wavier. The Agency provided a response on January 30, 2023, conveying their disagreement with the request and stating that a pre- and post-natal developmental study to assess postnatal effects following in utero and lactational exposure would be needed to support a marketing application. The Agency’s response also added that a juvenile animal study would be needed to support the development of sepiapterin in children and that carcinogenicity studies would be needed to support labeling for sepiapterin. On January 11, 2023, PTC amended protocol PKU-004 (version 5.0) to include two new cohorts of PKU patients who did not participate in study PKU-003. The Agency issued an information request on February 3, 2023, to question whether future drug development would be negatively impacted by adding these new patient cohorts. PTC provided a response on February 17, 2023, indicating the additional cohorts would not impact future development and that the additional participants and study sites would allow for the development of a robust population PK model and exploration of the exposure-response relationship for all age groups. A revised protocol for PKU-004 (version 6.0) was also included with their response. PTC subsequently amended protocol PKU-004 (version 8.0) on February 1, 2024. In preparation for PTC’s planned NDA for sepiapterin, CMC-specific, type C written responses were issued to IND 143698 on January 15, 2023, providing feedback on the regulatory starting material designation for the commercial drug substance. Type C written responses were also issued on May 15, 2023, providing advice on PTC’s planned integrated summary of safety and Bioresearch Monitoring data package for their planned NDA submission. A TQT study waiver was requested by PTC under IND 143698 on February 14, 2023. The Agency responded on May 18, 2023, that an evaluation of the QTc response at high clinical exposures would be necessary to waive the need for a TQT study. PTC also requested a carcinogenicity waiver on March 20, 2023. Following a review of PTC’s weight of evidence document which was proposed in lieu of conducting a 2-year rat carcinogenicity study, the Agency informed PTC on June 2, 2023, that the neoplastic and preneoplastic findings observed with sepiapterin in rats necessitated a 2-year rat carcinogenicity study. The Agency added that although the 2-year rat carcinogenicity study could be conducted as a postmarketing requirement, the report of the 26-week transgenic mouse study should be provided in the NDA to support product labeling. A second Preliminary BTDR Advice teleconference was held for the proposed PKU indication on June 28, 2023, during which PTC was informed that, in the absence of data from an active control trial of sufficient duration (i.e., at least one month of Kuvan treatment), it would be difficult to interpret the available efficacy data and conclude that sepiapterin offered substantial improvement over existing therapies for PKU. Reference ID: 5631809

NDA 219666 SEPHIENCE (sepiapterin) 135 Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23) A type B, Pre-NDA meeting was held on September 8, 2023, to discuss the content and format of PTC’s proposed marketing application for a PKU indication for sepiapterin. During the meeting, the Agency reiterated that a 6-month transgenic mouse study and QT assessments for both sepiapterin and BH4 should be provided with the NDA. Meeting minutes were issued on October 6, 2023. On September 29, 2023, PTC submitted a request for a carcinogenicity special protocol assessment. An advice letter was issued on October 27, 2023, emphasizing the Agency’s recommendation to submit the final report, or a draft audited report with signed pathology report, for a 6-month mouse carcinogenicity study no later than the NDA submission. The carcinogenicity special protocol assessment was agreed to by the Agency on November 8, 2023. On September 14, 2023, the Agency informed PTC that their proposed proprietary name, SEPHIENCE, was conditionally acceptable. On November 21, 2023, PTC submitted a new protocol and statistical analysis plan to IND 143698 for a QT study, PTC923-TQT-102-HV (version 1.0), titled “A Randomized, Placebo- Controlled Study to Evaluate the Safety, Tolerability, Pharmacokinetics, and Concentration-QTc Effects of Sepiapterin in Healthy Adults.” The Agency issued comments pertaining to this protocol on January 4, 2024, and a revised protocol (version 2.0) was submitted by PTC on February 12, 2024. On July 29, 2024, PTC submitted NDA 219666 under section 505(b)(1) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act for sepiapterin oral powder, a new molecular entity to be marketed using the proposed proprietary name SEPHIENCE, for the treatment of HPA in pediatric and adult patients with PKU. The NDA was considered filed on September 27, 2024, and received a standard review timeline. 13. Pharmacology Toxicology 13.1. Executive Summary Sepiapterin, also known as PTC923; formerly CNSA-001, is a PAH enzyme activator that is rapidly metabolized in the liver to BH4 via the pterin salvage pathway (Mayer and Werner 1995). Sepiapterin primarily acts as a precursor of the enzymatic co-factor BH4 to activate PAH (Ohashi et al. 2011; Werner et al. 2011). Exogenously delivered sepiapterin leads to significant increases in hepatic BH4. Once the liver compartments are saturated, circulating (plasma) levels of BH4 increase rapidly and significantly, ultimately resulting in an increased PAH activity in patients with PKU. Two drugs have been approved for PKU: pegvaliase-pqpz is approved as monotherapy for adults with PKU, and sapropterin dihydrochloride, which is structurally related to sepiapterin, is approved in conjunction with dietary management for pediatric (>1 month) and adults with PKU. In addition to the present IND, the Applicant has also submitted PKU (IND 143698). The Applicant has also cross- referenced nonclinical studies submitted under and IND 143698 to support NDA 219666. provenancePages.text: NDA 219666 SEPHIENCE (sepiapterin) 135 Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23) A type B, Pre-NDA meeting was held on September 8, 2023, to discuss the content and format of PTC’s proposed marketing application for a PKU indication for sepiapterin. During the meeting, the Agency reiterated that a 6-month transgenic mouse study and QT assessments for both sepiapterin and BH4 should be provided with the NDA. Meeting minutes were issued on October 6, 2023. On September 29, 2023, PTC submitted a request for a carcinogenicity special protocol assessment. An advice letter was issued on October 27, 2023, emphasizing the Agency’s recommendation to submit the final report, or a draft audited report with signed pathology report, for a 6-month mouse carcinogenicity study no later than the NDA submission. The carcinogenicity special protocol assessment was agreed to by the Agency on November 8, 2023. On September 14, 2023, the Agency informed PTC that their proposed proprietary name, SEPHIENCE, was conditionally acceptable. On November 21, 2023, PTC submitted a new protocol and statistical analysis plan to IND 143698 for a QT study, PTC923-TQT-102-HV (version 1.0), titled “A Randomized, Placebo- Controlled Study to Evaluate the Safety, Tolerability, Pharmacokinetics, and Concentration-QTc Effects of Sepiapterin in Healthy Adults.” The Agency issued comments pertaining to this protocol on January 4, 2024, and a revised protocol (version 2.0) was submitted by PTC on February 12, 2024. On July 29, 2024, PTC submitted NDA 219666 under section 505(b)(1) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act for sepiapterin oral powder, a new molecular entity to be marketed using the proposed proprietary name SEPHIENCE, for the treatment of HPA in pediatric and adult patients with PKU. The NDA was considered filed on September 27, 2024, and received a standard review timeline. 13. Pharmacology Toxicology 13.1. Executive Summary Sepiapterin, also known as PTC923; formerly CNSA-001, is a PAH enzyme activator that is rapidly metabolized in the liver to BH4 via the pterin salvage pathway (Mayer and Werner 1995). Sepiapterin primarily acts as a precursor of the enzymatic co-factor BH4 to activate PAH (Ohashi et al. 2011; Werner et al. 2011). Exogenously delivered sepiapterin leads to significant increases in hepatic BH4. Once the liver compartments are saturated, circulating (plasma) levels of BH4 increase rapidly and significantly, ultimately resulting in an increased PAH activity in patients with PKU. Two drugs have been approved for PKU: pegvaliase-pqpz is approved as monotherapy for adults with PKU, and sapropterin dihydrochloride, which is structurally related to sepiapterin, is approved in conjunction with dietary management for pediatric (>1 month) and adults with PKU. In addition to the present IND, the Applicant has also submitted PKU (IND 143698). The Applicant has also cross- referenced nonclinical studies submitted under and IND 143698 to support NDA 219666. Reference ID: 5631809 (b) (4) (b) (4) (b) (4)

NDA 219666 SEPHIENCE (sepiapterin) 136 Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23) The nonclinical safety profile of sepiapterin supporting this NDA was evaluated in (1) primary and secondary pharmacology studies, (2) safety pharmacology studies, (3) PK/ADME studies, (4) repeated dose toxicity studies in rats (up to 6 months) and marmosets (up to 9 months), (5) a standard battery of in vitro and in vivo genotoxicity studies, (6) dose-ranging reproductive and developmental toxicity studies including embryo-fetal developmental studies in rats and rabbits, and fertility studies in male and female rats, (7) peri- and postnatal developmental study in rats and juvenile animal studies in rat, (8) impurities studies, (9) carcinogenicity studies in transgenic mice (6-month), and (10) a phototoxicity study. The 2-year carcinogenicity bioassay was not included in this submission. Even though there was a negative finding in the 6-month transgenic mouse carcinogenicity study, there were sepiapterin-related proliferative (hypertrophy, pre- /neoplastic) histopathologic findings observed in a standard battery of tissues in chronic repeated dose toxicity studies, including three pituitary tumors in the rat study (2 HD males and 1 HD recovery female) and several incidences of hyperplasia/metaplasia/hypertrophy in other tissues. In addition, pituitary tumors are mechanistically related to the pheochromocytomas observed in the 2-year rat carcinogenicity study of the approved drug KUVAN. Because PKU causes significant morbidity, and patients with PKU face substantial health complications, which leads to care and social burden and the high unmet medical need, the 2-year carcinogenicity study will not be required prior to approval but will be a post-marketing requirement study. 13.2. Summary Review of Studies Submitted With the Investigational New Drug Application The nonclinical studies submitted in the IND are described individually below. Each were reviewed previously in the respective reviews by Dr. Patil (DARRTS, October 20,2017), Dr. McLeod-Flynn (DARRTS, October 19,2021), Dr. Harrouk (DARRTS, December 14,2022); Dr. Tsai-Turton (DARRTS, February 03,2023; March 21,2023; May 23,2023), Dr. Agyeman (DARRTS, November 21,2023; April 18,2024, and Dr. Ahir (DARRTS, June 27, 2025). 13.3. Individual Reviews of Studies Submitted With the New Drug Application 13.3.1. Pharmacology Study Title: Sepiapterin Treatment Trial in PAH-R261Q Mice Key Study Findings The Applicant performed a non-GLP single dose PKU mouse model Pah-R261Q study to determine the effects of sepiapterin for treatment of PKU (Study Report Reference No. PTC923- 2024-114). A single dose of sepiapterin was administered by oral gavage to PKU mice before a Phe challenge was administered by intraperitoneal injection (Table 54). At doses of 10, 30, and 100 mg/kg, sepiapterin resulted in a dose-dependent decrease in elevated blood Phe levels and increase in PAH enzyme activity in this mouse model induced by a phenylalanine challenge (Figure 18 and Figure 19). This study supports the potential mode of action of sepiapterin. Reference ID: 5631809

PTC provided a response on February 17, 2023, indicating the additional cohorts would not impact future development and that the additional participants and study sites would allow for the development of a robust population PK model and exploration of the exposure-response relationship for all age groups. A revised protocol for PKU-004 (version 6.0) was also included with their response. PTC subsequently amended protocol PKU-004 (version 8.0) on February 1, 2024. In preparation for PTC’s planned NDA for sepiapterin, CMC-specific, type C written responses were issued to IND 143698 on January 15, 2023, providing feedback on the regulatory starting material designation for the commercial drug substance. Type C written responses were also issued on May 15, 2023, providing advice on PTC’s planned integrated summary of safety and Bioresearch Monitoring data package for their planned NDA submission. A TQT study waiver was requested by PTC under IND 143698 on February 14, 2023. The Agency responded on May 18, 2023, that an evaluation of the QTc response at high clinical exposures would be necessary to waive the need for a TQT study. PTC also requested a carcinogenicity waiver on March 20, 2023. The Agency added that although the 2-year rat carcinogenicity study could be conducted as a postmarketing requirement, the report of the 26-week transgenic mouse study should be provided in the NDA to support product labeling. A second Preliminary BTDR Advice teleconference was held for the proposed PKU indication on June 28, 2023, during which PTC was informed that, in the absence of data from an active control trial of sufficient duration (i.e., at least one month of Kuvan treatment), it would be difficult to interpret the available efficacy data and conclude that sepiapterin offered substantial improvement over existing therapies for PKU. Reference ID: 5631809

Nonclinical Assessment of Potential Effectiveness The pharmacodynamic effects of doxecitine and doxribtimine were assessed in Tk2 knockout or Tk2 H126N knock-in mouse models of TK2d in which both alleles of the Tk2 gene are inactivated by homologous recombination. Oral gavage administration was used in all primary pharmacodynamic studies, which were conducted to evaluate the efficacy of doxecitine and doxribtimine by assessing incorporation of exogenous doxecitine and doxribtimine into mtDNA and effects on mtDNA copy number and animal survival. These studies demonstrated that orally administered doxecitine and doxribtimine 1) incorporated into mtDNA of mouse skeletal muscle; 2) increased mtDNA copy number in tissues, including the skeletal muscle, of TK2d mice; and 3) extended the lifespan of TK2d mice by approximately 2- to 3-fold. Refer to Sections 6.3.2, 13.1, and 13.2 for a detailed review of these studies. Reference ID: 5687706

provenancePages.text: NDA 219792 Kygevvi (doxecitine and doxribtimine) 12 Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23) Product and Mechanism of Action Doxecitine and doxribtimine are both pyrimidine nucleosides. The proposed mechanism of action of this two-drug combination is the balanced increase of substrate levels of both deoxynucleosides: doxecitine and doxribtimine, bypassing the impaired TK2 salvage pathway pyrimidine nucleotide synthesis in TK2d. The incorporation of the exogenous doxecitine and doxribtimine into mtDNA leads to increased mtDNA copy number in target tissues including skeletal muscle (Lopez-Gomez et al. 2017; Blázquez-Bermejo et al. 2019). Additionally, in study MT1621-19-014, when TK2 knockout and wild-type mice were treated with MT1621 with stable isotope labelled dC or dT (“heavy” dC containing 3 N15 atoms and 3 amu heavier compared to endogenous “light” dC; “heavy” dT containing 2 N15 atoms and 2 amu heavier compared to endogenous “light” dT), “heavy” nucleosides were incorporated into mitochondrial DNA. Incorporation of these heavy nucleosides in MT1621-treated mice was statistically significant compared to mice treated with phosphate-buffered saline, for both genotypes (wild-type [WT] and Tk2KO mice). These results supported the proposed mechanism of action for MT1621; a combination of dC and dT was incorporated into mtDNA. Thus, there was a compelling rationale for developing this two-drug combination for the treatment of TK2d and it was reasonable for the Applicant to evaluate the combination compared to untreated patients to establish effectiveness. Key Regulatory History In terms of regulatory history, orphan drug designation was granted to a combination of deoxycytidine monophosphate (dCMP) and deoxythymidine monophosphate (dTMP) for the treatment of TK2d on July 7, 2016. The Applicant submitted their IND 134037 and opening protocol to FDA on December 14, 2018. The program was developed to support the use of good manufacturing practice (GMP)-quality drug for the treatment of TK2d primarily through the comparison of treated subjects from a retrospective medical chart review, and open-label trial, and untreated subjects identified in the literature. A request for Breakthrough Therapy designation was granted on February 8, 2019. On September 1, 2022, the Applicant submitted a meeting request to discuss the proposed dosing components for the administration of the drug product and to discuss the completed clinical and nonclinical programs intended to support a future marketing application. The type B pre-NDA teleconference was held on November 17, 2022 (meeting minutes issued December 5, 2022). The application encompasses two retrospective medical chart review studies, one single-arm trial, and the expanded access program of patients with TK2d. The integrated summary of efficacy from these studies is proposed as the adequate and well-controlled investigation (AWCI). Note: For ease of reading, we will use, from this section onward, the terms doxecitine and doxribtimine to refer to all formulations of the study drug including:  dC/dT: pyrimidine nucleosides deoxycytidine and deoxythymidine  dCMP/dTMP: pyrimidine nucleotides deoxycytidine monophosphate and deoxythymidine monophosphate  Doxecitine and doxribtimine: GMP-manufactured doxecitine and doxribtimine Reference ID: 5687706

provenancePages.text: BLA 761391 NEMLUVIO (nemolizumab-ilto) 120 Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23) 13. Pharmacology Toxicology 13.1. Summary Review of Studies Submitted With the Investigational New Drug Application The nonclinical studies conducted to support nemolizumab were originally submitted to and reviewed under IND 117122. All pertinent studies were also submitted to the present BLA. CIM331 and CH5427227 were the code names for nemolizumab used in nonclinical studies. 13.1.1. Pharmacology (Primary and Secondary) Nemolizumab is a humanized monoclonal IgG2 antibody recognizing IL-31RA and blocking binding of IL-31. An engineered IgG2 structure was adopted to reduce effector function. IL-31 is a cytokine produced by activated T cells, and it belongs to the IL-6 cytokine family. IL- 31 signals through a heterodimeric receptor, consisting of IL-31RA and the oncostatin M receptor (OSMR) beta chain. Subsequently the down-stream JAK/STAT signaling pathway is activated and the signal is transmitted into the cell. IL-31 has been identified as a cytokine that induces pruritus, barrier disruption, skin inflammation, and fibrosis. Studies have shown that IL- 31 plays a role in several skin diseases including atopic AD and PN. By blocking IL-31 signaling, nemolizumab is expected to ameliorate itching and skin inflammation in AD and PN patients. In Vitro Studies Nemolizumab binds to human and cynomolgus monkey IL-31RA with high affinity [dissociation constant (KD): 0.374 and 0.191 nM, respectively]. Nemolizumab inhibits the binding of IL-31 to human or monkey IL-31RA in a concentration-dependent manner. Nemolizumab inhibited human IL-31-dependent proliferation of the cell line BaF/2C6/16 which was transfected with human IL-31RA and OSMR genes, in a concentration-dependent manner. Similarly, nemolizumab also inhibited monkey IL-31-dependent proliferation of the cell line Ba/F3 which was transfected with monkey IL-31RA and OSMR genes. Mepolizumab inhibited IL-31-induced STAT3 phosphorylation in an IL-31RA-expressing human cell line (A549) in a concentration-dependent manner. Nemolizumab also inhibited IL- 31-induced IL-6 production, MMP-1 production, MMP-3 production, and apoptosis in a human epidermal keratinocyte cell line (HaCaT) in a concentration-dependent manner. In the TF-1 cell line, nemolizumab did not affect the cell proliferation induced by IL-6 or OSM, which are cytokines that utilize gp130, a cytokine receptor that has homology to IL-31RA. The binding of nemolizumab to human Fcγ receptor and monkey Fcγ receptor was measured by surface plasmon resonance and compared to panitumumab (a control antibody with human IgG2 constant regions) and rituximab (a control antibody with human IgG1 constant regions). The results showed that the binding of nemolizumab, which has modified human IgG2 constant regions, to human Fcγ receptor is similar to that of panitumumab and much weaker than that of rituximab. The results suggested that the risk of antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC) associated with nemolizumab was likely lower than that for IgG1. Reference ID: 5495495

provenancePages.text: BLA 761391 NEMLUVIO (nemolizumab-ilto) 116 Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23) III. Additional Analyses and Information 12. Summary of Regulatory History Biologics License Application (BLA) 761391 for NEMLUVIO (nemolizumab-ilto) for the treatment of atopic dermatitis (AD) was submitted under section 351(a) of the Public Health Service (PHS) Act on December 13, 2023. The associated investigational new drug (IND) (117122) was submitted on September 10, 2013, by Chugai Pharmaceuticals Co. The IND was transferred to Galderma Research and Development, LLC on December 9, 2016. Nemolizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody of the IgG2 subclass that inhibits IL-31 signaling by binding to the IL-31 receptor alpha (IL-31R). The Applicant submitted BLA 761390 simultaneously for the treatment of prurigo nodularis (PN). This approach was discussed during the two pre-BLA meetings which took place on April 24, 2023, for the AD indication and April 26, 2023, for the PN indication. The PN indication was approved August 12, 2024, for the pre- filled pen, 30 mg/0.49 mL presentation at which time the proprietary name of NEMLUVIO was approved. The Agency has had ongoing communication via meetings and specific correspondence with the Applicant regarding the development program for the AD indication as summarized below. • February 20, 2013, Pre-IND meeting. • November 22, 2013: IND 117122 Study May Proceed. • August 5, 2014, Pediatric Study Plan - Written Response. • July 2, 2014, chemistry, manufacturing, and control (CMC) Meeting: to discuss Chemistry, Manufacturing and Controls nemolizumab (CIM331) development program. • March 13, 2017, Guidance Meeting: The Agency agreed that the proposed doses are supported by the available clinical safety data. The Agency expressed concern that the pruritus visual analog scale endpoint and the exposure-response relationship from pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PKPD) modeling were the basis for the dose selection and stated that phase 2 dose-ranging trials should include the efficacy endpoints that will be used in the phase 3 studies. The initial Pediatric Study Plan (iPSP) should be submitted for review. The Agency agreed that the Sponsor’s plan to request a waiver for the Thorough QT/QTc study but continue to perform electrocardiograms (ECGs) for safety appeared reasonable. The Agency agreed that the existing nonclinical and clinical data appear to support the proposed phase 2b dose-ranging study. The Agency requested that the Sponsor should revise their proposed Eczema Area and Severity Index (EASI) score in order that patients with moderate-to-severe disease will be enrolled. The proposed use of topical corticosteroids (TCS) as adjunctive therapy to nemolizumab and the choice of TCS and proposed TCS regimen during run-in period and during treatment period of the study appeared to be acceptable. The Agency asked for additional qualitative and quantitative evidence to support the relevance of the Sleep Disturbance NRS. The Agency expressed concerns regarding the SCORing Atopic Dermatitis (SCORAD) design. • July 6, 2017, PSP – Initial No Agreement. Reference ID: 5495495

Healthy subjects versus patients PK was similar between healthy subjects and subjects with AD. Drug exposure at steady state following the therapeutic dosing regimen (or single dose, if more relevant for the drug) Parameter Mean  SD AUC 117 ± 46.0 μg•day/mL for subjects receiving 60 mg loading dose followed by 30 mg every 4 weeks (Q4W) and 34.2 ± 17.4 μg•day/mL for subjects receiving 60 mg loading dose followed by 30 mg every 8 weeks (Q8W). Cmax 5.59 ± 1.95 μg/mL for subjects receiving 60 mg loading dose followed by 30 mg Q4W and 1.92 ± 0.84 μg/mL for subjects receiving 60 mg loading dose followed by 30 mg Q8W. C24 2.63 ± 1.27 μg/mL for subjects receiving 60 mg loading dose followed by 30 mg Q4W and 0.74 ± 0.44 μg/mL for subjects receiving 60 mg loading dose followed by 30 mg Q8W. Range of effective dose(s) or exposure In the phase 2a study (Study CIM003JG), 0.5 mg/kg and 2.0 mg/kg dose administered Q4W achieving marked reduction of pruritus visual analogue scale (VAS) compared to 0.1 mg/kg in subjects with AD. Although the study was not designed to compare the different dose groups formally, there was no evidence that 2.0 mg/kg nemolizumab administered Q4W or Q8W was more effective than the 0.5-mg/kg Q4W dose. In the phase 2b study (114322) in subjects with AD, nemolizumab 30 mg Q4W (with 60 mg loading dose) was statistically significantly more effective than placebo in reducing Eczema Area and Severity Index (EASI) scores at Week 24. The most marked effects on secondary endpoints of PP-NRS and Investigator’s Global Assessment (IGA) scores were also seen in nemolizumab 30 mg Q4W compared with placebo. The phase 2 study results suggested that a plateau of efficacy was achieved with the 30 mg Q4W dose (with 60 mg loading dose), and no additional benefit was expected with a higher dose. In the pivotal phase 3 trials (Studies 118161 and 118169), an initial dose of 60 mg followed by 30 mg given Q4W was superior to placebo with respect to the co-primary endpoints of IGA success and EASI-75. Maximally tolerated dose or exposure The highest studied single dose was 3 mg/kg in the first-in-human (FIH) Study CIM001JP. The highest-studied multiple dose was 60 mg Q4W using the to-be-marketed formulation. Dose proportionality After a single dose, nemolizumab exposure increased dose proportionally over a dose range between 0.03 and 3 mg/kg following subcutaneous administration. After multiple doses, nemolizumab systemic exposure increased in an approximately dose-proportional manner across the subcutaneous dose range up to 30 mg. There was a slight decrease in bioavailability by 9% with the 60 mg subcutaneous dose and by 15% with the 90 mg subcutaneous dose. Accumulation The accumulation index (Rac) of nemolizumab following multiple-dose administration was 1.6, calculated using Population PK analysis. Time to achieve steady- state For subjects receiving nemolizumab 30 mg SC Q4W with a 60 mg SC loading dose, steady-state was reached by Week 4. Bridge between to-be- marketed and clinical trial/study formulations In the phase 3 trials in subjects with AD (Studies 118161, 118169, and 118163), nemolizumab was supplied as a lyophilized powder in a dual-chamber syringe (DCS) for solution for injection, which held the lyophilized nemolizumab or placebo and the sWFI separately. provenancePages.text: BLA 761391 NEMLUVIO (nemolizumab-ilto) 24 Integrated Review Template, version 4.0 (11/1/23) Characteristic Drug Information mild or moderate hepatic impairment was observed on nemolizumab PK. However, due to limited data, the impact of severe hepatic impairment on the PK of nemolizumab is unknown. Drug Interaction Liability (Drug as Perpetrator) Inhibition/induction of metabolism The formation of CYP450 enzymes can be altered by increased levels of certain cytokines (e.g., IL-1, IL-6, IL-10, TNFα, IFN) during chronic inflammation. Treatment with nemolizumab may modulate serum levels of some cytokines and influence the formation of CYP450 enzymes. Therefore, the Applicant conducted a phase 2, open-label, single-sequence, drug-drug interaction (DDI) study in adult subjects with moderate-to-severe AD to evaluate the effect of nemolizumab on the PK of a drug “cocktail” representative of cytochrome P450 (CYP450) sensitive index substrates (CYP1A2, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2D6, and CYP3A4/5). Results of this study showed that for all CYP substrates, the observed geometric means for both Cmax and AUC were similar before and after nemolizumab treatment, with geometric mean test/reference ratios ranging from 88.24% to 107.81%. There was no clinically meaningful effect of nemolizumab treatment on the metabolism of the assessed CYP substrates, defined as a greater than 2-fold decrease of observed geometric means after nemolizumab injections, indicating that nemolizumab is unlikely to affect the expression of CYP enzymes. Inhibition/induction of transporter systems NA Immunogenicity (if Applicable) Bioanalysis A validated anti-drug antibody (ADA) assay method using a homogeneous electrochemiluminescence (ECL) format with the MesoScale Discovery (MSD) platform was applied for testing of antibody testing in all clinical studies. Incidence In the pivotal trials in subjects with AD (Studies 118161 and 118169) and the long-term extension (LTE) study in subjects with AD (Study 118163), the incidence of treatment-emergent ADAs was 11.2% (46 out of 358 subjects). Clinical impact Antidrug antibodies (ADAs) to nemolizumab were associated with reduced serum nemolizumab concentrations beyond Week 16. In the phase 3 trials, nemolizumab treated subjects who developed ADAs had nemolizumab concentrations that were 20% to 70% lower compared to subjects who did not develop ADAs. There was no clinically significant effect of ADAs on safety or efficacy of nemolizumab over the treatment duration of 48 weeks. INTRODUCTION Regulatory History • Nipocalimab is a neonatal Fc receptor blocker that was originally developed by Momenta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. for the treatment of gMG. Momenta Pharmaceuticals was later acquired by Johnson & Johnson in 2020 and is now considered a part of Janssen Research & Development, LLC. • Nipocalimab for the treatment of gMG was granted Orphan Drug Designation on February 11, 2021, and Fast Track Designation on December 21, 2021. • On August 29, 2024, the applicant, Janssen Biotech, submitted a new biologic application for nipocalimab intravenous injection via 505(b)(1) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, for the treatment of gMG in adults and adolescent patients, 12 years and older, who are antibody positive. o In this submission, the applicant also included a study report from a Phase 2 study, MOM-M281-003, in pregnant women at high risk for early onset severe hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn. Janssen Biotech is currently developing nipocalimab for treatment of pregnant women at high risk for early onset severe hemolytic disease of fetus and newborn • On September 23, 2024, DN1 consulted DPMH to assist with the Pregnancy and Lactation Labeling Rule (PLLR) sections of labeling. This is a priority review. BACKGROUND The Role of the Neonatal Fc Receptor The neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) belongs to the family of major histocompatibility complex molecules. FcRn binds to IgG and albumin with high affinity at low pH, and it regulates the serum half-lives of both proteins. FcRn protects circulating IgG and albumin from early degradation and plays an important role in immunity at mucosal and systemic sites through both its ability to affect the lifespan of IgG as well as its participation in innate and adaptive immune responses. 2 In polarized cells such as the epithelium, FcRn is able to transport IgG bi- directionally via transcytosis. Summary Review of Studies Submitted With the Investigational New Drug Application The nonclinical safety studies conducted to support MK-1654 (clesrovimab) were originally submitted to and reviewed under IND 130097. All pertinent studies were also submitted to the present BLA and are reviewed in this section. 13.1.1. Pharmacology 13.1.1.1. Primary Pharmacology MK-1654 is a human anti-RSV F protein IgG1 monoclonal antibody. It is identical to its predecessor, RB-1, except for YTE substitutions in its Fc region (M252Y/S254T/T256E) which increases neonatal Fc receptor binding affinity and serum half-life. MK-1654 and RB-1 bind to the same epitope on the F protein with similar affinities. MK-1654 demonstrated antiviral activity in cotton rats, and the breadth of activity has been demonstrated across temporally distinct RSV isolates. See the virology review (refer to Section 18) for more information. 13.1.1.2. Secondary Pharmacology The binding affinity of MK-1654 to human and rhesus monkey red blood cells and platelets was evaluated in vitro. MK-1654 binding was similar to controls in both cell types and species at the concentrations and conditions tested. No binding of clinical concern to red blood cells and platelets was observed. 13.1.1.3. Safety Pharmacology Safety pharmacology of MK-1654 was assessed as a component of the GLP 2-week repeat dose toxicology study in Wistar Han rats (Study # TT #16-1029). In that study, functional observational battery performed on the first six males from each IV group, approximately 1 hour following the first dose on Day 1, showed no treatment-related adverse effects on functional nervous system parameters at all dose levels tested (up to 300 mg/kg). There was a slight decrease in overall activity (19% and 26% decrease in the number of lines crossed in the 100 mg/kg and 300 mg/kg groups, respectively) during the open-field observations. These findings were within historical control limits and were not associated with other findings, so were considered incidental. In addition, there were no clinical signs nor microscopic findings indicating any MK-1654 related effects on the central nervous system, cardiovascular or respiratory systems in rats. Refer to the GLP 2-week toxicology study review in Section 13.1.2.1 for more information. Reference ID: 5604981

William Tubbs Executive Director, Regulatory Affairs, Visterra, Inc. 1.0 BACKGROUND Sibeprenlimab is a humanized IgG2 monoclonal antibody (mAb) directed against A Proliferation Inducing Ligand (APRIL) that blocks the binding of soluble APRIL to its receptors, transmembrane activator and calcium modulator and cyclophilin ligand interactor (TACI) and B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA). APRIL regulates B-cell- mediated immune responses through several mechanisms, including playing a role in class switch recombination and T-cell independent production of immunoglobulin A in mucosa. Sibeprenlimab is being studied as a potential treatment for biopsy-confirmed immunoglobulin A nephropathy (IgAN) and is intended for chronic use to prevent progression of this condition to kidney failure. Visterra requested this meeting to obtain feedback on the design of their phase 3 trial and the clinical and nonclinical data packages proposed for licensure. Preliminary responses to the submitted questions were provided to the Sponsor, and are copied below, followed by any additional discussions that took place during the Reference ID: 4907313 Reference ID: 5704038

IND 135282 Page 3 U.S. Food and Drug Administration Silver Spring, MD 20993 www.fda.gov meeting. The Sponsor used the appended slide presentation to guide the discussion. The meeting discussion focused on questions 1, 2, 3, 4 and 7. 2.0 DISCUSSION 2.1 Clinical Question 1: Does the agency agree that a significant reduction in proteinuria relative to placebo at 9 months, as measured by the uPCR from 24-hour urine collection, is a clinically meaningful surrogate endpoint to support Accelerated Approval of sibeprenlimab for the treatment of IgAN? Question 2: Does the agency agree that for the phase 3 Trial 417-201-00007, measuring the difference in eGFR slope over approximately 24 months in the sibeprenlimab-treated group compared with the placebo-treated group is acceptable as the clinical endpoint for confirmatory approval? Preliminary FDA Response to Questions 1 and 2: In brief, you propose a single phase 3 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (417-201-00007) in approximately 484 adults with biopsy-confirmed IgAN on stable, maximally tolerated renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) blockade for at least 3 months, urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) ≥0.75 g/g or urine protein ≥1 g/day, and an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) ≥30 mL/min/1.73 m2. Patients will be randomized 1:1 to sibeprenlimab or placebo administered as a subcutaneous injection once every 4 weeks for 26 doses (until Week 100). Randomization will be stratified by screening UPCR (≤2 g/g vs >2 g/g), eGFR (30-44 vs ≥45 mL/min/1.73 m2), and sodium- glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor (SGLT2i) use (yes or no). The study will exclude patients with nephrotic syndrome, a serum IgG level <500 mg/dL, or a mesangial cellularity, endocapillary proliferation, segmental sclerosis, tubular atrophy (MEST) or MEST-crescents (MEST-C) score of T2 or C2 on kidney biopsy. The proposed primary endpoint is the ratio of 24-hour UPCR at 9 months to baseline. The key secondary endpoint is eGFR slope over approximately 24 months. You plan to request accelerated approval based on the primary endpoint, and subsequent full approval based on the key secondary endpoint. We have the following general comments on the design of a development program to support accelerated approval for the treatment of IgAN. We encourage you to consider requesting a follow-up meeting after you have given further thought to these issues, as well as our statistical comments. a. We would accept a substantial reduction in proteinuria as a reasonably likely surrogate endpoint in IgAN and as a basis for accelerated approval. However, to support accelerated approval, the magnitude of the treatment effect on proteinuria would need to be sufficient to provide confidence that the post-marketing phase of Reference ID: 4907313 Reference ID: 5704038

This power calculation should be based on a quantitative model of the relationship between the endpoint that will be used to support accelerated approval and the endpoint that will be used to verify the benefit in patients with IgA nephropathy. b. Your power calculations for the confirmatory phase of your trial should account for sources of uncertainty including uncertainty in the treatment effect on proteinuria and the uncertainty in the relationship between treatment effects on proteinuria at 9 months and treatment effects on eGFR. Note that an effect on proteinuria that barely excludes no effect leaves insurmountable uncertainty in the predicted effect on eGFR. For this reason, we believe it is important to power your trial to provide greater precision around the estimate for the treatment effect on proteinuria. Sponsor Response: See attached slides Discussion during the meeting: The Sponsor provided an overview of their proposed statistical approach for phase 3 (see slides 5 and 6). The Sponsor indicated that data on the relationship between proteinuria at 9 months and 2-year total eGFR slope from the Inker, et al publication (AJKD vol. 78 Iss. 3 Sep 2021) were used to power the trial such that the proposed study had at least 95% power to detect a 30% reduction in UPCR at 9 months. The Division acknowledged that the Inker publication provides important information on the relationship between changes in proteinuria at 9 months and 2-year eGFR slope and recommended that the Sponsor use the size of the treatment effect on UPCR seen in their phase 2 trial to power the phase 3 trial. The Division emphasized that showing a statistically significant effect on UPCR would not be sufficient to support accelerated approval. There would also need to be confidence that the confirmatory phase of the trial was adequately powered to verify the benefit, taking into account the various sources of uncertainty (see preliminary responses above). The Division request that the Sponsor submit information on the treatment effect on UPCR and eGFR seen in phase 2 when the data become available, as well as information on the model used to predict treatment effects on eGFR, including how the model handles the various sources of uncertainty. The Division explained that it would need this information to determine whether the Sponsor’s assumptions for powering the confirmatory phase of the study are reasonable. provenancePages.text: IND 135282 Page 11 U.S. Food and Drug Administration Silver Spring, MD 20993 www.fda.gov Preliminary FDA Response: We agree, in principle, that a single adequate and well-controlled trial plus confirmatory evidence could be used to satisfy the regulatory requirement for substantial evidence of effectiveness. Discussion during the meeting: None. Question 10: Does the agency agree that the anticipated patient exposure data at the time of Biologics License Application submission provides sufficient data for regulatory decision making? Preliminary FDA Response: You anticipate approximately 219 patients with IgAN will be exposed to multiple doses of sibeprenlimab in the phase 2 and 3 clinical trials at the time of BLA submission for proposed accelerated approval (approximately 219 patients should have >6 months exposure, approximately 82 patients >12 months, and approximately 82 patients >24 months). We recognize that the size of your safety data will be limited by the size of the affected population; whether the safety database is adequate will be determined as part of the NDA review. Discussion during the meeting: None. Question 11: Does the agency agree with the current method to assess anti-drug antibodies and the proposed method to assess neutralizing anti-drug antibodies? Preliminary FDA Response: Based on the limited information provided in the meeting package, your current method to detect anti-drug antibodies (ADA) and the proposed approach to detect neutralizing anti-drug antibodies (NAb) are reasonable. In addition, the drug tolerance of your immunogenicity assays will be confirmed once the steady state concentration of sibeprenlimab from the pivotal clinical study is known. Per FDA Guidance for Industry, Immunogenicity Testing of Therapeutic Protein Products —Developing and Validating Assays for Anti-Drug Antibody Detection (2019), FDA recommends that screening and confirmatory ADA assays achieve a sensitivity of at least 100 ng/mL ADA positive control with on board drugs. Ensure that validated method performance parameter ranges different from those recommended in the FDA guidance, e.g., MRD of 1:4, and parameters recommended for validation by the guidance that are not included in your validation exercise, are adequately addressed and justified in your validation report. IND 135282 Page 12 U.S. Food and Drug Administration Silver Spring, MD 20993 www.fda.gov Discussion during the meeting: None. 2.1. Clinical Pharmacology Question 12: The proposed dosing regimen for the phase 3 trial (417-201-00007) is 400 mg of sibeprenlimab administered SC once every 4 weeks. Does the agency agree with the proposed dosing regimen for the phase 3 trial determined by PK/Pharmacodynamic modeling and simulation? Preliminary FDA Response: You propose a dosing regimen of 400 mg sibeprenlimab administered subcutaneously (SC) once every four weeks in the proposed phase 3 trial. Your dose selection is based on the reduction in serum IgA (approx. 60%) achieved with monthly doses of 4 mg/kg administered intravenously (IV) to patients with IgAN. Based on the population PK/PD modeling, the 400 mg SC dose is expected to provide similar PK and IgA reduction compared to the 4 mg/kg IV dose. We agree that your proposed dosing regimen appears reasonable; however, it may be prudent to also use the dose-response data on UPCR that will be obtained from your phase 2 trial to inform dose selection and ensure that the selected dose of 400 mg SC is optimal (and that a higher dose is not needed). Discussion during the meeting: None. Question 13: The sponsor proposes to allow injection site flexibility in the phase 3 trial including upper arm, abdomen, and thigh. Does the agency agree the proposed plan will provide sufficient information to support a label that provides for the injection sites specified? Preliminary FDA Response: None. We agree with your proposal to allow flexibility in injection site including upper arm, abdomen, and thigh, in the phase 3 trial. Assuming adequate data from each injection site, the proposed approach could support a label that specifies each of these sites, provided injection site is not a significant covariate on the PK or PD of sibeprenlimab. Question 14: Does the agency agree that the contents of the clinical pharmacology package are sufficient for approval of sibeprenlimab? Reference ID: 4907313 Reference ID: 5704038

Discussion during the meeting: None. 2.2. Nonclinical Question 15: Does the agency agree that the completed and proposed nonclinical program is adequate for approval? Preliminary FDA Response: Yes, we agree that the completed and proposed nonclinical program appear to be adequate for a BLA submission. Discussion during the meeting: None. 2.3. Chemistry, Manufacturing, and Controls Question 16: Two receptor-blocking (BCMA and TACI) enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays representing the sibeprenlimab mechanism of action were developed and qualified for sibeprenlimab potency assessment. Does the agency agree that a single potency assay of TACI receptor blocking is adequate for phase 3 development and approval? Preliminary FDA Response: We do not have sufficient information to determine whether a single TACI receptor blocking assay is adequate for phase 3 development and approval. We have the following comments about your proposal: a. The current sibeprenlimab drug substance (DS) and drug product (DP) specifications include an APRIL-binding ELISA assay as a potency assay. It is not clear whether you plan to replace the current APRIL-binding ELISA assay or to add the proposed TACI receptor blocking assay as an additional potency assay. In your meeting package, you indicate that “additional receptor-blocking potency assays were developed” to “augment the APRIL-binding ELISA assay”. Please clarify whether you plan to use two potency assays for release and stability testing. Note that in addition to method validation, bridging data between the current and the proposed potency assays will be needed to replace any assay. b. You have not justified why the TACI receptor blocking assay was chosen over the BCMA receptor blocking assay, or addressed whether APRIL binding to TACI, BCMA, or both is relevant to clinical efficacy in the proposed patient population. In addition, we note slight differences in Figure 20 between the IC50 values of APRIL- TACI binding and APRIL-BCMA binding inhibition by sibeprenlimab. Office of Study Integrity and Surveillance (OSIS) An OSIS audit request was requested for Study HLX14-001. The study was conducted at three clinical sites and used one analytical site: • Clinical site 1: Huashan Hospital, Shanghai, China • Clinical site 2: Shuguang Hospital, Shanghai, China • Clinical site 3: Wuxi People's Hospital, Wuxi, China • Analytical site: Shanghai Jollin Lab Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China The Office of Study Integrity and Surveillance (OSIS) determined that inspections are not needed for Clinical site 1 (Huashan Hospital, Shanghai, China) and Clinical site 2 (Shuguang Hospital, Shanghai, China). The rationale for this decision is that although OSIS has no prior inspection history for these sites, inspections are not needed because OSIS had an inspection for the other clinical site (Clinical site 3, Wuxi People's Hospital, Wuxi, China) listed on the consult which enrolled the majority of subjects for the study, and which will provide some assurance of the overall conduct of the study. (refer to OSIS review dated June 26, 2025, in DARRTS). The inspection for the analytical site at Shanghai Jollin Lab Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China, has been completed and no objectionable conditions were observed (refer to OSIS review dated June 27, 2025, in DARRTS). The inspection for the clinical site at Wuxi People's Hospital, Wuxi, China has been completed. Objectionable conditions were found during the inspection and Form FDA 483 was issued at the inspection close-out. There was also one discussion item addressed at the close of the inspection. After reviewing the inspectional findings, the exhibits provided in EIR, and the clinical investigator’s response to Form FDA 483 and the discussion item, OSIS had concerns regarding the safeguarding the rights and welfare of human subjects, specifically with respect to the site’s provision of false information during the medical counseling of a subject and his partner, which appears to have resulted in termination of a pregnancy conceived during the subject’s participation of the study. OSIS also concluded there were two regulatory violations under 21 CFR 312. However, the observations and discussion item do not impact the reliability of the data for inspected study HLX14-001. (refer to OSIS review dated July 10, 2025, in DARRTS). Reference ID: 5647489

The nonclinical toxicity of denosumab is related to its affinity to RANKL and related biological activity. Thus, in vitro physicochemical, and functional characterizations of denosumab products are considered sufficient and more sensitive than animal studies to detect any functional differences (e.g., in affinity to RANKL and receptor activity) between HLX14 and reference products. The Applicant has conducted in vitro functional evaluations, testing for immunochemical properties (FcγR, FcRn and C1q binding) and in vitro biological activity (RANKL binding, neutralization activity, inhibition of osteoclast differentiation, ADCC-NK, and CDC) and other testing as part of the Comparative Analytical Assessment. The physicochemical characterization and functional activity studies support that HLX14, US- Prolia, and US-Xgeva are highly similar. See full review by Office of Product Quality Assessment 3 (OPQA3). Reference ID: 5647489

INTRODUCTION The Division of Pulmonary, Allergy and Rheumatology Products (DPARP) consulted the Division of Pediatric and Maternal Health (DPMH) on October 26, 2015, to provide input for appropriate labeling of the pregnancy and lactation subsections of Humira (adalimumab) to comply with the Pregnancy and Lactation Labeling Rule (PLLR) format. REGULATORY HISTORY Humira (adalimumab) is a recombinant human IgG1 monoclonal antibody specific for human tumor necrosis factor (TNF) and is indicated for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis (RA), juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), psoriatic arthritis (PsA), ankylosing arthritis (AS), (CD), Ulcerative Colitis (UC), Plaque Psoriasis (Ps) and Hidradenitis Suppurativa. Humira was approved in the US on December 31, 2002. On September 3, 2015, AbbVie submitted an efficacy supplement for Humira (adalimumab), BLA 125057/S­ 397, for a new indication for the treatment of non-infectious intermediate, posterior and panuveitis in adult patients. AbbVie also updated labeling to comply with the PLLR format. BACKGROUND Adalimumab and Drug Characteristics Adalimumab binds to TNF-alpha and blocks its interaction with p55 and p75 cell surface TNF receptors. TNF is a naturally occurring cytokine that is involved in normal inflammatory and immune responses. TNF is increased in patients with RA, JIA, PsA, and 2

provenancePages.text: 2.1.2 History of Drug Development Adalimumab was first approved in the US and EU for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) in 2002 and 2003, respectively, and in more than 90 countries world-wide since. Additional indications have been approved in the US and EU, and globally, including PsA, AS, ulcerative colitis (UC), JIA, adult and pediatric Crohn's disease (CD), and adult and pediatric psoriasis (Ps). Studies in adult active and inactive non-infectious intermediate uveitis, posterior uveitis, and panuveitis patients treated with adalimumab were initiated in August 2010. A pre-Phase 3 Type B Meeting was held between the FDA (Division of Anti-Infective and Ophthalmology Products) and Abbott (now AbbVie) on 18 September 2009. Further clarification and agreement were reached through a conference call held on 08 March 2010. The Agency generally agreed to the design of the studies, as well as inclusion criteria, dosing, corticosteroid tapering, and statistical analysis plan. The phase 3 study protocols were submitted to the FDA under IND 105723. 2.1.3 Studies Reviewed HUMIRA® non-infectious unvietis clinical development plan included three clinical studies. Two of these studies (Studies 877 and 880) were pivotal, randomized, double-masked clinical studies. In addition, there is one ongoing open-label safety study ± Study M11-327. Study 877 (VISUAL I) was a multicenter, randomized, double-masked, placebo-controlled study of the efficacy and safety of the human anti-TNF monoclonal antibody adalimumab as maintain therapy in subjects requiring high dose corticosteroids for active non-infectious intermediate-, posterior-, or pan-uveitis. Study 880 (VISUAL II) was a multicenter, randomized, double-masked, placebo-controlled study of the efficacy and safety of the human anti-TNF monoclonal antibody adalimumab in subjects with inactive non-infectious intermediate-, posterior-, or pan-uveitis. Study M11-327 is an ongoing open-label, multicenter, long-term safety and efficacy study of adult subjects with non-infectious intermediate uveitis, posterior uveitis, or panuveitis who participated in Studies M10-877 or M10-880 and who either discontinued from the study for having met the endpoint of treatment failure or completed the study without treatment failure at Week 80 or remained in the study until it was stopped (completed < Week 80 but subjects had to terminate the study because the planned number of treatment failures was reached). This statistical review focused on the two pivotal safety and efficacy studies: Studies M10-877 and M10-880 (also referred to as Study 877 and Study 880 throughout this review). provenancePages.text: sNDA Multi-disciplinary Review and Evaluation {NDA 208573, S-009} {VENCLEXTA (Venetoclax)} Review Strategy The key materials used for the review of efficacy and safety include: • NDA 208573 • IND 110159 • Relevant published literature • Relevant information in the public domain The review of efficacy was primarily based on analysis of patients treated on Study M14-358 for venetoclax in combination with azacitidine or decitabine and on Study M14-387 for venetoclax in combination with LDAC. Data from both trials was used to support dose selection for each combination. All efficacy results were verified by independent analysis, except where indicated. Efficacy evaluations were conducted using the following efficacy populations (summarized in Table 21): • All patients treated at the proposed labeled dose of venetoclax in each combination • Patients in each treatment combination who met the modified Ferrara criteria to identify patients whose age or comorbidities preclude the use of intensive induction chemotherapy. See Trial Designs for details on these criteria. • Additional patients enrolled who did not have known comorbidities that preclude the use of intensive therapy but were enrolled prior to defining the criteria. Table 21: Patient enrollment in each efficacy population by treatment combination Venetoclax (400 mg) + Azacitidine Venetoclax (400 mg) + Decitabine Venetoclax (600 mg) + LDAC Overall 84 31 82 Modified Ferrara Yes 67 13 61 Modified Ferrara No 17 18 21 The description of the treatment combination in the indication proposed by the Applicant was for venetoclax in combination with hypomethylating agents or low-dose cytarabine. For the purposes of this review, the two HMAs, azacitidine and decitabine, are considered two independent combination and not HMAs as a class. While the HMAs have a similar mechanism of action, the efficacy and safety profiles of each differ. Efficacy of venetoclax monotherapy for treatment of relapsed/refractory AML was reviewed from Study M14-212. Because an indication for the treatment of patients with r/r AML was not sought, independent analyses were not verified for this study. Only summary results are provided for Study M14-212. 56 Version date: September 12, 2018 Reference ID: 4352694

The Sponsor is therefore planning to conduct a definitive drug-drug interaction study to evaluate the potential interaction between CBD and everolimus. The protocol for this study (GWCP19195) has been submitted to IND 120055 (Sequence 0529). Rapamycin (mTOR inhibitors, e.g., everolimus, sirolimus) or Calcineurin Inhibitors (e.g., tacrolimus) are also substrates for P-glycoprotein (P-gp). Cannabidiol is not a substrate for P-gp but it has been shown to be a weak inhibitor. The Ki value for CBD was determined to be in excess of 1.83 μM. Therefore, the role of P-gp inhibition in the gastrointestinal tract as a potential mechanism for an interaction with P-gp substrates such as everolimus, especially given the high doses of CBD administered and the enhanced solubility in its oil formulation cannot be ruled out. Inhibition of intestinal P-gp may increase absorption by blocking efflux transport and decrease total metabolism, resulting in a significant increase in intestinal bioavailability of these drugs. CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS: Labeling recommendations-based literature reports should include following statement “Mechanism of increase in mTOR or calcineurin inhibitors concentrations is not clearly understood” until the study GWCP19195 report is submitted to the FDA’s review. Labeling Revisions: 7.4 Concomitant Use of EPIDIOLEX and Mammalian Target of Rapamycin (mTOR) or Calcineurin Inhibitors No dedicated drug-drug interaction studies have been conducted with mTOR inhibitors (e.g., everolimus) or calcineurin inhibitors (e.g., tacrolimus). Reports in the literature suggest that cannabidiol administration resulted in increased serum levels of everolimus, sirolimus or tacrolimus. Mechanism of increase in mTOR or calcineurin inhibitors concentrations is not clearly understood. Consider a reduction in dosage of everolimus, sirolimus or tacrolimus, if adverse reactions are experienced when co-administered with EPIDIOLEX. Jagan Mohan Parepally, M.S., Ph.D. Reviewer Division of Neuropsychiatric Pharmacology (DNP) Michael Bewernitz, Ph.D. Reviewer Division of Pharmacometrics (DPM) Reference ID: 4645734

Kaler, MD, MPH, CAPT (Retired), USPHS; Professor, Center for Gene Therapy, Nationwide Children’s Hospital, Columbus, OH 1.0 BACKGROUND FDA Regulatory Background Cyprium Therapeutics, Inc. (Cyprium) is developing copper histidinate for the treatment of Menkes disease. Copper histidinate is a sterile lyophilized product reconstituted with normal saline and is intended to be administered subcutaneously to infants and children The Sponsor has had multiple interactions with the Agency to discuss the program development plan since the opening of the IND in 1989. Major regulatory milestones are summarized in the table below. Initial IND • December 28, 1989- Initial IND for copper histidinate for the treatment of Menkes disease was opened as a research IND. IND 034166 was placed on full clinical hold on January 29, 1990. • May 31, 1990- A complete response for the clinical hold issues was received. • FDA removed Clinical Hold on June 18, 1990. Administrative • October 11, 2005- IND 034166 was transferred from the Division of Metabolism and Endocrinology Products to the Division of Gastroenterology Products (DGIEP), from which the Division of Rare Diseases and Medical Genetics (DRDMG) emanated, and where the IND now resides. • May 14, 2012- Orphan drug designation granted for copper histidinate for the treatment of Menkes disease. Reference ID: 4682260 (b) (4) (b) (4) (b) (4) (b) (4) (b) (4)

IND 034166 Page 3 U.S. Food and Drug Administration Silver Spring, MD 20993 www.fda.gov • June 25, 2018- Fast Track designation was granted for copper histidinate for patients diagnosed with classic Menkes disease who have not demonstrated significant clinical progression. • January 17, 2019- Change of Sponsor: IND sponsorship was transferred from Dr. Stephen Kaler, National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD), part of the National Institutes of Health (NIH), to Cyprium. Meetings • December 16, 2015- A Type B, guidance meeting was held to discuss the prospect of a New Drug Application (NDA) for copper histidinate for the treatment of Menkes disease. FDA outlined the required data to support an NDA, particularly requiring a natural history study in lieu of internal controls study to demonstrate efficacy. Meeting minutes were issued on December 28, 2015. • July 11, 2017- A Type B, guidance meeting was held to further discuss the clinical development program for copper histidinate. FDA provided feedback on the sponsor’s proposed plan to use data from clinical trials, study 90-CH-0149 titled “Copper Histidinate Therapy in Menkes Disease” and 09-CH-0059 titled “Molecular Bases of response to Copper Treatment in Menkes Disease, Related Phenotypes, and Unexplained Copper Deficiency,” to support an NDA. Agreement was reached on the survival analysis as the primary endpoint. In addition to comments on the clinical trials design, FDA provided feedback on the proposed plan for safety, non-clinical, clinical pharmacology, CMC, and statistics. Meeting minutes were issued on July 13, 2017. • February 7, 2018- A Type C, guidance meeting was held to discuss the sponsor’s proposed primary efficacy analysis for the NDA. FDA also provided comments on the proposed PK study waiver and biomarkers of pharmacodynamic response. Meeting minutes were issued February 28, 2018. • September 26, 2018- A Type C, guidance meeting with Dr. Kaler (NIH) and Cyprium was held to further discuss the planned primary efficacy analysis. FDA suggested the Sponsor to submit a Statistical Analysis Plan (SAP) for review. Meeting minutes were issued on October 23, 2018. • June 19, 2019- A Type B, guidance meeting was held to discuss the first draft of the SAP version 1.0, titled “Comparison of Menkes Disease Patients Treated with Copper Histidinate to Untreated Historical Control Patients,” received on May 17, 2019. Agreement was reached that the primary efficacy analysis will be survival from date of birth. A sensitivity analysis will explore survival by date of birth adjusted for gestational age. Meeting minutes issued were on June 23, 2019. Reference ID: 4682260

provenancePages.text: DIVISION OF ANTIVIRAL PRODUCTS (HFD-530) VIROLOGY REVIEW NDA#: 216964 SDN:001 DATE REVIEWED STARTED: 04/29/2025 2 Structure Drug category: Antiretroviral Indication: Treatment of HIV-1 infection Dosage Form/Route of administration: once daily oral FDC tablet Supporting documents: IND134036 (Fixed-dose combination of DOR/ISL), IND128595 (ISL), IND112796 (DOR) Abbreviations: 3TC, lamivudine; ARV, antiretrovirals; DOR, doravirine: DTG, dolutegravir; FDC, fixed-dose combination; FTC, emtricitabine; GFP, green fluorescent protein; HIV-1, human immunodeficiency virus type 1; ISL, islatravir, MK-8591; INSTI, integrase strand transfer inhibitor; IQ, inhibitor quotient; MFI, mean fluorescence intensity; NNRTI, non-nucleos(t)ide analog HIV-1 reverse transcriptase inhibitor; NRTI, nucleos(t)ide analog HIV-1 reverse transcriptase inhibitor; PBMC, peripheral blood mononuclear cell; PI, protease inhibitor; RNA, ribonucleic acid; RT, reverse transcriptase; TAF, tenofovir alafenamide; TP, triphosphate EXECUTIVE SUMMARY This is an Original NDA for the combination of the approved non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI) doravirine (DOR) and the investigational nucleoside analog reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) islatravir (ISL) for the treatment of HIV-1 infection in virologically suppressed adults submitted on April 28, 2025. Merck is cross referencing the DOR (PIFELTRO™) NDA 210806 that was first approved by the FDA on August 30, 2018, which provides for the use of DOR in combination with other antiretroviral agents for the treatment of HIV-1 infection in adult patients with no prior antiretroviral treatment history. The indication for DOR was expanded to include patients who are virologically suppressed (HIV-1 RNA less than 50 copies per mL) on a stable antiretroviral regimen with no history of treatment failure and no known substitutions associated with resistance to DOR on September 19, 2019. Doravirine is a pyridinone NNRTI of HIV-1 and inhibits HIV-1 replication by non-competitive inhibition of HIV-1 reverse transcriptase (RT). Doravirine demonstrated antiviral activity against a broad panel of primary HIV-1 isolates (subtypes A, A1, AE, AG, B, BF, C, D, G, H) with EC50 values ranging from 1.2 nM to 10.0 nM. Observed emergent RT amino acid substitutions in DOR-resistant strains included: V106A, V106I, V106M, V108I, H221Y, F227C, F227I, F227L, F227V, M230I, L234I, P236L, and Y318F, which conferred 3.4-fold to 70-fold reductions in susceptibility to DOR. These treatment-emergent DOR resistance-associated substitutions can confer cross resistance to efavirenz, etravirine, nevirapine, and rilpivirine. Clinical isolates containing the Y188L substitution alone or in combination with K103N or V106I, V106A in combination with G190A and F227L, or E138K in combination with Y181C and M230L showed greater than 100-fold reduced susceptibility to DOR Reference ID: 5760091

DIVISION OF ANTIVIRAL PRODUCTS (HFD-530) VIROLOGY REVIEW NDA#: 216964 SDN:001 DATE REVIEWED STARTED: 04/29/2025 3 This review encompasses the assessment of ISL drug classification, nonclinical data for ISL (antiviral activity, cytotoxicity, cell culture combination evaluations, resistance and cross- resistance evaluations in cell culture), ISL-induced lymphocyte toxicity, and DOR and ISL resistance data from clinical studies P051 and P052. Islatravir Nonclinical Virology The applicant proposed to classify islatravir (ISL) in a new class as a nucleoside reverse transcriptase translocation inhibitor (NRTTI). Their position is that ISL is structurally and mechanistically different from NRTIs. The Division maintains that ISL belongs in the NRTI class and does not warrant a new classification as a NRTTI because ISL’s structure, mechanism of action, and mode of resistance is the same as other NRTIs. Similar to other NRTIs, ISL acts by preventing translocation of the primer:template in the RT active site and preventing binding of incoming dNTPs resulting in chain termination. In addition, ISL has cross-resistance with lamivudine and emtricitabine with the same resistance substitutions, M184V or I, and ISL has also shown resistance to thymidine analog mutation substitutions (TAMs), which confer resistance to other NRTIs. In a biochemical assay using purified recombinantly expressed HIV-1 reverse transcriptase (RT), ISL-triphosphate inhibited HIV-1 reverse transcriptase with an IC50 value of 346 ± 59 nM (n=17). In cell culture assays, ISL exhibited EC50 values <1 nM against wild-type laboratory strains of HIV-1 in MT-4 cells, PBMCs and monocyte-derived macrophages. ISL demonstrated antiviral activity against a panel of 50 primary HIV-1 isolates (subtypes A, A1, AE, AG, B, BF, C, D, F1, G, H) with EC50 values ranging from 2.4 nM to 6.9 nM. The median EC50 value against the subtype B isolates was 4.3 nM (range 3.0 nM-5.3 nM) (n=6). Islatravir did not show any antiviral activity against other viruses (HBV, HCV, Bovine viral diarrhea virus, Dengue-2 virus, Zika virus, Yellow fever virus, Respiratory syncytial virus, Coxsackie B virus, Rhinovirus 14, Venuzuelan equine encephalitis virus, Herpes Simplex virus 1, Influenza A and B viruses, and Enterovirus) but showed weak antiviral activity with EC50 values of 34.8 and 22.3 μM against human Cytomegalovirus and Vaccinia virus, respectively ISL demonstrated little or no toxicity at concentrations <12 μM in proliferating cell lines and primary cell cultures. CC50 values were comparable in activated and resting primary cells. The CC50 value observed for activated PBMCs is >100,000-fold greater than the ISL EC50 value of 0.00021 μM required for antiviral activity in human PBMCs. However, decreases in lymphocytes and CD4+ T cell counts were seen in the DOR/ISL clinical trials at the 0.75 mg dose of ISL and the FDA placed the DOR/ISL IND on partial clinical hold on December 10, 2021, due to risk of ISL leading to decreased lymphocyte and CD4+ T cell counts. The applicant submitted substantive investigations into the mechanism of the lymphocyte decreases. They identified a plausible mechanism for the decreases in lymphocyte and CD4+ T cell counts observed with the 0.75 mg ISL dose in the clinical trials, and a threshold level (i.e., 0.25 mg dose) for ISL-triphosphate (TP) below which decreases in lymphocyte cell counts are not expected to be observed. The proposed mechanism is that high concentrations of ISL-TP preferentially accumulate in lymphocytes resulting in cell growth inhibition and apoptosis: Reference ID: 5760091

Cytotoxicity of ISL on Activated and Resting PBMCs with Cladribine as the Positive Control for Normalization to Maximal Cytotoxicity Source: Report PD030, page 12 ASSESSMENT OF LYMPHOCYTE TOXICITY Decreases in lymphocytes and CD4+ T cell counts were seen in the DOR/ISL clinical trials and the FDA placed the DOR/ISL IND on partial clinical hold on December 10, 2021, due to risk of ISL leading to decreased lymphocyte and CD4+ T cell counts. The applicant conducted substantive investigations into the mechanism of the lymphocyte decreases. They identified a plausible mechanism for the decreases in lymphocyte and CD4+ T cell counts observed with ISL doses in clinical trials, and a threshold level (i.e., 0.25 mg dose) for ISL-TP below which decreases in lymphocyte cell counts are not expected to be observed. The leading hypothesis is that high concentrations of ISL- triphosphate (TP) preferentially accumulate in lymphocytes resulting in cell growth inhibition and apoptosis, and that mitochondrial toxicity is not a contributing mechanism for the decrease in lymphocytes. The following evidence supports this plausible mechanism for the decreases in lymphocyte and CD4 T+ cell counts observed with ISL in clinical trials: Evidence of Preferential Accumulation of ISL-TP in Lymphocytes ISL-TP, like other deoxyadenosine analogs, is preferentially accumulated in lymphocytes. There are at least three factors leading to this selective accumulation in lymphocytes compared to other tissues. • First, lymphocytes have a high ratio of deoxycytidine kinase (dCK) to 5’ nucleotidase enzyme gene expression compared to other tissues. dCK adds the rate-limiting first phosphate group to ISL starting the anabolism cascade that eventually leads to ISL-TP. Once nucleosides (including ISL) are phosphorylated, the phosphorylated forms (mono-, di-, and tri-phosphate) cannot readily diffuse out of the cell. The high ratio of dCK to 5’ nucleotidases (5’ nucleotidases remove phosphate groups from phosphorylated ribonucleotide and deoxynucleotide molecules) in lymphocytes is likely to contribute to the accumulation of ISL-TP in these cells. • Second, lymphocytes contain high levels of adenosine deaminase (ADA), which metabolizes adenosine and deoxyadenosine to inosine and deoxyinosine, respectively. passages.text: DIVISION OF ANTIVIRALS, CDER/OND/OID CLINICAL VIROLOGY REVIEW NDA 216964 (Original NDA) eCTD REVIEW COMPLETED: 12/3/2025 BACKGROUND DOR+ISL is a fixed-dose combination of doravirine (DOR, 100 mg), an approved NNRTI, and islatravir (ISL, 0.25 mg), an investigational NRTI, being developed as a complete regimen for the treatment of HIV-1 infection in adults and adolescents. DOR was approved for the treatment of HIV-1 infection in combination with other antiretroviral agents (PIFELTRO, N210806) and as a fixed-dose combination with lamivudine and tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (both NRTIs) (DELSTRIGO, N210807) in 2018. Potential advantages of DOR+ISL relative to other antiretroviral therapy (ART) regimens include potent antiviral activity (including activity against common NRTI- and NNRTI-resistant variants), different mechanisms of action, non-overlapping and complementary resistance profiles, lack of food requirements, and a favorable drug-drug interaction profile. This review summarizes the sponsor’s analyses and independent FDA analyses of DOR+ISL resistance in 3 ongoing Phase 3 studies of DOR+ISL as a treatment for HIV-1 infection in virologically suppressed adults with no history of virologic treatment failure or known/documented DOR resistance (V106A/M, V108I, Y188L, H221Y, P225H, F227C/L/V, M230I/L, L234I, P236L, Y318F): studies P051, P052, and P054.
